1. Philosophy and design principles

Verse is a high-level, statically typed, general-purpose language whose single overriding goal is readability. A Verse program should read like a short, clear piece of prose: you should be able to show it to a colleague who has never seen the language and have them follow along.

Everything else in the language follows from a handful of principles.

1.1 Code is read far more often than it is written

Verse optimizes for the reader. Keywords are short English words (mut, if, for, match, with, and, or, not). Punctuation is used only where it carries real meaning. Blocks are marked by indentation, so the visual shape of the code is its structure.

1.2 Minimal punctuation, maximal meaning

There are no semicolons, no braces around blocks, and no parentheses around conditions. The punctuation that remains stands for one idea each. Some marks are used in several places, but always for the same idea — the table lists every use honestly:

Symbol Meaning
( ) "group": calls, parameters, tuples, grouping, variant fields
[ ] "position": list literals, indexing, slicing, list patterns
{ } "contents": map literals ({"a": 1}, empty {:}), set literals (set{…}), and — inside text — interpolation ("{name}")
< > "type parameter": generics
-> "produces": lambdas and match arms (nothing else)
| "one of": variants, union and error types (Int | Error), pattern alternatives
? "maybe missing or failed": T? (a type that may be missing), postfix expr? (stop early on error or missing), and the pattern x? (match a present value)
: "has type" or "is named": type annotations, return types, record fields, named arguments, map entries, supertraits and generic constraints (T: Order), typed patterns (n: Int), field patterns (age: 18), loop labels (outer:), and interpolation format specifiers ({price:.2})

1.3 Safe by default

  • There is no null. A value that might be absent has an optional type T?, and the compiler makes you handle the absence.
  • Errors are values in the type: a function that can fail says so in its signature (Int | Error), and failure must be handled or explicitly propagated with ?. Silently discarding a fallible result is a compile-time error; _ = … is the visible way to ignore one on purpose.
  • Types are static but visually optional: the compiler infers them — including function parameters and return types — and when it cannot decide, it stops and asks for one annotation at that exact spot. It never guesses.
  • Bindings are immutable unless marked mut: x = 1 binds a name that never changes, mut count = 0 one that can. A name is bound once per function — there is no shadowing — so x = … on a name that already exists can only be an assignment to a mut binding.
  • Every value has exactly one owner and is freed deterministically when its owner's scope ends. There is no garbage collector, no manual allocation, no pointer or reference you can write down, no dangling reference and no use-after-free. Functions borrow their arguments unless they say mut (exclusive, mutable) or take (consume).
  • Integer overflow, out-of-bounds list indexing and division by zero stop the program with a clear message rather than silently producing garbage.
  • Concurrency is race-free by construction: a task owns what it is given; sharing between tasks happens only through opt-in handles (channels, Shared, Guarded).

1.4 One obvious way

Verse prefers one clear construct per idea. There is one loop over collections (for ... in), one general branching construct for data (match), one way to mark public items (export), and one official formatter (verse fmt) whose output is the canonical style.

1.5 Scripts grow into programs

A Verse file is a script: statements run from top to bottom, no ceremony and no main function required. The same file can grow functions, types, tests and modules without ever being rewritten into a "real program" shape.

1.6 Tests and documentation are part of the language

Doc comments (##) and test blocks (test "name") are first-class syntax, not conventions. The tooling understands them directly.

1.7 Notation in this document

Code blocks are Verse unless marked otherwise. Inside examples, ... stands for code that has been left out for brevity; it is not Verse syntax. Comments of the form # 3 show what a line prints or evaluates to.

2. Quick tour

The following program shows most of Verse on one page. It reads a list of people, greets them, and summarizes some facts.

## A small tour of Verse.

import read_text from std.fs

type Person
    name: Text
    age: Int
    email: Text? = none

type Shape = Circle(radius: Float) | Square(side: Float)

# Types are optional. This function is fully inferred…
fn greet(person, greeting = "Hello")
    "{greeting}, {person.name}!"

# …and this one spells its types out. Both are statically checked.
fn area(shape: Shape): Float
    match shape
        Circle(r) -> 3.14 * r * r
        Square(s) -> s * s

fn parse_age(text: Text): Int | Error
    age = text.trim().to_int()?
    if age < 0
        return error("age cannot be negative: {age}")
    age

# `mut` borrows exclusively; `take` consumes the argument.
fn add_guest(mut list, take guest)
    list.push(guest)

mut people = [
    Person(name: "Ana", age: 30, email: "ana@example.com"),
    Person(name: "Bruno", age: 17),
]
add_guest(mut people, Person(name: "Carla", age: 41))

for person in people                      # each person is borrowed
    print(greet(person, greeting: "Welcome"))
    print("  contact: {person.email otherwise "no email"}")

adults = people.filter(p -> p.age >= 18).map(.name.copy())
label = if adults.len() == 1 then "adult" else "adults"
print("{adults.len()} {label}: {adults.join(", ")}")

bruno_email = people.find(p -> p.name == "Bruno").email otherwise "none"
print("Bruno's email: {bruno_email}")

total = [Circle(radius: 1.0), Square(side: 2.0)].map(area).sum()
print("Total area: {total:.2}")

mut count = 0                             # `x = …` binds once; `mut` can change
for i in 1..=10
    if i % 2 == 0
        count += 1
print("{count} even numbers between 1 and 10")

mut first = "Ana"
mut second = "Bruno"
(first, second) = (second, first)         # both are `mut`: a swap
print("{first}, then {second}")

config = spawn read_text("config.txt")
print(config.wait() otherwise "no config found")

test "greeting uses the given name"
    ana = Person(name: "Ana", age: 30)
    assert greet(ana) == "Hello, Ana!"

test "negative ages are rejected"
    assert parse_age("-3") is _: Error
    assert parse_age(" 42 ")? == 42

Run it with verse run tour.vs; run its tests with verse test tour.vs. Two things are worth noticing. greet and add_guest have no type annotations at all, yet everything is checked at compile time (§4.2). And the .copy() in the adults line is the one place ownership shows: filter passes views of the people along without copying anything, and the chain ends in map, whose result is a new list that must own its names — so each name is copied, visibly (§4.9, §9.5).

3. Lexical structure and syntax

3.1 Source files

A Verse source file is UTF-8 text with the extension .vs. Each file is a module (see §12). Line endings may be \n or \r\n.

3.2 Comments

# A line comment runs to the end of the line.

## A doc comment documents the item that follows it.
## It may span several lines and uses Markdown.
fn square(n: Int): Int
    n * n
  • # starts an ordinary comment.
  • ## starts a doc comment. A block of ## lines directly above a declaration (no blank line in between) documents that declaration (fn, type, alias, trait, impl, a module constant, a field, or a test).
  • A ## block at the very top of a file that is followed by a blank line is the module doc. verse fmt enforces the blank line, so the two cases always look different. See §14.3.

There are no block comments; the formatter and editors handle commenting out regions.

3.3 Indentation and blocks

Blocks are introduced by a line that ends a header (such as if cond, for x in xs, fn f(), type T, match v) and consist of the following lines that are indented further.

if temperature > 30
    print("Hot")
    print("Stay hydrated")
else
    print("Pleasant")

Rules:

  • Indentation uses spaces only; a tab character in leading whitespace is a compile-time error. The canonical width is 4 spaces.
  • A block's lines must all share the same indentation.
  • An empty block is not allowed; write pass when a block intentionally does nothing.

3.4 Line continuation

A statement normally ends at the end of a line. It continues onto the next line when:

  1. the line ends inside an open (, [, or {; or
  2. the line ends with a binary operator (+, and, or, otherwise, ==, **, …); or
  3. the next line begins with . after a complete expression (a method chain); or
  4. the next line begins with | (the next alternative of a variant list, §4.4).

A line that ends with -> opens an indented block instead: the body of a match arm, or — inside an open ( — the body of a lambda. In the lambda case the dedent that ends the block also closes the ( opened on that line (the closing rule, §5.4).

A leading dot that starts an expression (right after (, , or an operator) is not a continuation but a key-path lambda such as .name (§5.4).

A type X = header always continues on the same logical line; it never opens a field block. Only a header of the form type X (or type X<T>) with nothing after the name opens an indented block of fields.

report = orders
    .filter(o -> o.paid)
    .map(o -> o.total)
    .sum()

ok = user.active and
    user.verified

point = Point(
    x: 1.0,
    y: 2.0,
)

Trailing commas are allowed everywhere a comma-separated list appears.

3.5 Identifiers and naming

Identifiers start with a letter or _ and continue with letters, digits or _. Unicode letters are allowed. The first character decides what kind of name it is, and the compiler relies on this:

  • An identifier whose first letter is an uppercase letter (Unicode category Lu or Lt) is a type-level name: a type, variant, trait, or generic parameter.
  • Every other identifier — starting with a lowercase letter, _, or a letter that has no case at all (for example 数量 or مدينة) — is a value-level name: a variable, constant, function, field, parameter, or module.
Kind Style Example
Variables, functions, fields, modules snake_case user_count, read_text
Constants (module-level bindings) snake_case (same as variables) max_retries
Types, variants, traits, generic parameters PascalCase HttpClient, NotFound, Speaker, T

There is no SCREAMING_CASE: MAX_RETRIES = 3 is an error, because names are snake_case; capitalised names are types and patterns. Within those two kinds, snake_case and PascalCase are conventions enforced by verse fmt --check.

A single _ is a wildcard: it discards a value in patterns and bindings.

3.6 Keywords

alias      and        as         assert     break      continue   else
export     false      fn         for        from       if         impl
import     in         is         let        match      mut        none
not        or         otherwise  pass       return     self       Self
set        spawn      take       test       then       trait      true
type       while      with

let is reserved but not used: Verse has no let (bindings are written x = … and mut x = …, §3.9), and the compiler answers a let with the error "let is not used in Verse; write x = …".

3.7 Literals

# Integers
42
1_000_000
0xFF
0o755
0b1010_0101

# Floats
3.14
6.02e23
1e-9                          # an exponent alone makes a Float
1_000.5

Right after a ., a digit sequence is always a single INT, never the start of a FLOAT: t.0.1 is the field 1 of the field 0 of t (nested tuple access), not t followed by . and 0.1. A number followed by . and an identifier lexes as an INT and a method call (10.seconds()); a float needs a digit after the dot (10.0), and 10. alone is an error.

# Booleans
true
false

# Characters
'a'
'\n'
'é'

# Text
"Hello, world"
"Hello, {name}!"              # interpolation
"""
    Multi-line text.
    Leading indentation is stripped.
    """
r"C:\raw\path\{not interpolated}"   # raw text

# Bytes
b"GET / HTTP/1.1\r\n"

# Missing value
none

# Collections
[1, 2, 3]                     # List<Int>
{"ana": 30, "bruno": 17}      # Map<Text, Int>
{:}                           # empty map
set{"a", "b"}                 # Set<Text>
set{}                         # empty set
[0, ..rest]                   # spread a list into a list literal
{..defaults, "port": 80}      # spread a map; later keys win
(1, "one")                    # (Int, Text) tuple

# Ranges
1..10                         # 1 up to 9
1..=10                        # 1 up to 10
nums[2..]                     # open-ended: only inside a slice
nums[..3]

A bare {} is a compile-time error: it does not say whether a map or a set is meant, and the message points to {:} (empty map) and set{} (empty set).

Spread. Inside a list, set or map literal, a prefix .. spreads another collection's elements into the new one: [0, ..rest, 99], set{..admins, "root"}, {..defaults, "port": 80}. In a map literal, when the same key appears more than once, the later entry wins, so overrides go after the spread. A prefix .. (nothing on its left, right after [, { or ,) never clashes with the infix range operator a..b. Spreading moves the elements out of the source, so the source must be at its last use (a temporary, or a binding not used afterwards). If the source is used later, the spread is a compile error that suggests spreading a copy, ..xs.copy(); nothing is copied silently (§9.5).

Open-ended ranges — a.. (from a to the end) and ..b / ..=b (from the start) — are allowed only inside slice brackets, such as nums[1..], nums[..3], name[..=2]. Everywhere else a range needs both ends, so for i in 1.. is an error.

3.7.1 Text escapes

Escape Meaning
\n, \t, \r newline, tab, carriage return
\\ backslash
\" double quote
\{, \} literal braces (not interpolation)
\0 NUL character
\u{1F600} Unicode scalar value by hex code

3.7.2 Interpolation

Inside an ordinary (non-raw) text literal, {expr} evaluates expr and inserts its textual form (via the Show trait, §10). Any expression is allowed. A text literal inside an interpolation is allowed one level deep ("{email otherwise "none"}"); interpolation inside such a nested literal is an error. An optional format specifier follows a colon. The format colon is the first : that is not inside a bracket (( ), [ ], { }) or a nested text literal, so "{f(x: 1)}" and "{ {"a": 1}["a"] }" contain no format specifier, while "{price:.2}" does. An expression whose own syntax has a top-level colon — such as a typed pattern in "{v is n: Int}" — must be wrapped in parentheses, "{(v is n: Int)}"; otherwise the colon is read as the format colon.

price = 1234.5
print("Total: {price:.2}")          # Total: 1234.50
print("Padded: {42:>6}")            # Padded:     42
print("Hex: {255:x}")               # Hex: ff
print("Contact: {email otherwise "none"}")

Style: keep nested literals short. A long expression or one with its own text literals reads better bound to a name first (label = if count == 1 then "item" else "items", then "{count} {label}"), and verse fmt --check suggests doing so.

3.7.3 Multi-line and raw text

A triple-quoted literal """ begins a multi-line text. The opening """ must end its line. The indentation of the closing """ is removed from every line, so multi-line text can be indented naturally with the surrounding code. Interpolation and escapes work as usual.

fn letter(name: Text): Text
    """
    Dear {name},

    Thank you for trying Verse.
    """

A raw literal r"..." or r"""...""" performs no escapes and no interpolation, so { and \ are ordinary characters — the form to use for JSON, regular expressions and Windows paths. r""" follows the same layout rules as """ (the opening quotes end their line; the closing indentation is removed). A single-line r"…" cannot contain ".

3.8 Operators and precedence

From highest to lowest binding:

Level Operators Associativity Notes
1 f(x) a[i] a.b a? left postfix, applied left to right (notes below)
2 ** right power; binds tighter than unary minus (§3.8.4)
3 -x right numeric negation
4 * / % left
5 + - left + also concatenates Text and lists
6 .. ..= none ranges
7 == != < <= > >= in not in is chained see §3.8.3
8 not right boolean negation
9 and left boolean, short-circuit
10 or left boolean, short-circuit
11 otherwise left fallback, short-circuit; restricted right operand (§3.8.2)

Notes on level 1:

  • A second postfix ? needs brackets: (x?)?.
  • a.b on an optional a follows the lifted-chain rule (§8.1).
  • Postfix ? is an ordinary postfix operator. A ? immediately followed by . (a?.b) is a compile-time error: "?. is not Verse; write (a?).b to propagate then read, or a.b otherwise … / a.b? to look through the optional". (find_user(id)?).email is valid: propagate a missing user out of the function, then read the field.

Three constructs are deliberately not operators in this table:

  • spawn is a prefix that applies to exactly one call expression (spawn fetch(url)); its operand is never an arbitrary expression, so it has no precedence to compare (§11).
  • if a then b else c is a complete expression form; each branch is a full expression, and the whole form extends as far to the right as possible. Wrap it in parentheses to use it inside a larger expression (§6.1). Right after return, break or continue, an if is always a postfix guard (§6.7): return if done means "return when done". To return a conditional value, parenthesize it: return (if c then a else b).
  • A lambda x -> expr likewise extends as far to the right as possible. A key-path lambda (.name) is a primary expression (§5.4).

Prefix .. (spread, §3.7) appears only directly inside a collection literal and is not an operator either.

Assignment (=, +=, -=, *=, /=, %=) is a statement, not an expression, so if x = 3 is always a syntax error.

3.8.1 Boolean operators: and, or, not

Boolean logic uses words, and only words: there is no &&, || or !. and, or and not accept only Bool operands — there is no "truthiness", so if items or name or "x" is a type error.

can_enter = is_member or has_ticket
valid = not name.is_empty() and age >= 18

and and or short-circuit.

3.8.2 The fallback operator: otherwise

left otherwise right means "use left if it is usable, otherwise right." The left operand must be optional or fallible:

Left operand type Fallback happens when… Result type
T? it is none T if right is T; T? if right is T?
T | E (E an error) it is an error T if right is T; T | E if right is T | E 
name = nickname otherwise "friend"                        # Text? → Text
timeout = settings["timeout"] otherwise 30                # Int? → Int
text = read_text(path) otherwise "default"                # Text | Error → Text
email = find_user(id).email otherwise "no email"          # User? → Text
source = read_text(primary) otherwise read_text(backup)       # still Text | Error

The right side is evaluated only when needed. Using otherwise on a value that can never be missing or failed (a plain Int, a Bool) is a compile-time error, because the fallback could never happen. The one exception is a binding with a refutable pattern (below): there the fallback runs when the pattern does not match, so the left side may be of any type (Circle(r) = shape otherwise return 0.0 with a plain Shape).

Ownership of the result. Either side of otherwise may be a view (a borrow, an element from find or m[k], §9.5) or an owned value. Text and number literals and other static data count as views when needed, so they fit either way. The result is:

Left Right Result
a view a view or a literal a view: args.first() otherwise "world"
owned owned, or a literal owned: read_text(path) otherwise "default"
a view an owned temporary (not static) owned, so the left side must be copied: m["k"].copy() otherwise make_default()
owned a non-static view owned, so the right side must be copied: read_text(path) otherwise fallback_text.copy()

Leaving out the .copy() in either of the last two rows is a compile-time error that names the side to copy. A view result follows the usual rules: it can be bound to a name as a local view or passed along, but storing or returning it needs .copy().

A literal in an owned position (the second row) is materialised: the compiler creates an owned value from it. This is the one implicit creation Verse allows, because it duplicates no user value. A lifted chain (§8.1) on an owned temporary yields an owned field, so in find_user(id).email otherwise "no email" (where find_user returns an owned User?) the left side is owned and the result is an owned Text.

The same rule applies to every expression that chooses between branches: if c then a else b, a block if/else used as a value, and the arms of a match. The result is a view only if every branch is a view (or a literal); otherwise it is owned, and each branch that is a view needs .copy() — a compile-time error otherwise.

otherwise binds more loosely than every other binary operator. To keep that from ever surprising a reader, the right operand of otherwise must be a literal (including a negative number such as -1), a call, a postfix expression (a name, field access, index, or a chain of them), a parenthesized expression, or another otherwise. Anything else is a compile-time error:

n = counts["a"] otherwise 0 + 1          # error: write `(counts["a"] otherwise 0) + 1`
                                         #        or `counts["a"] otherwise (0 + 1)`
count = counts.get("a", default: 0) + 1  # clearer still, for maps (§9.2)

otherwise return, otherwise break, otherwise continue

As a deliberate exception to that rule, the right operand of otherwise may also be one of the exits return (with or without a value), break or continue — but only as the whole right operand, never nested inside a larger expression:

fn label_for(id)
    user = find_user(id) otherwise return "unknown"         # User? → User
    "{user.name} ({user.age})"

for line in lines
    n = line.to_int() otherwise continue                    # skip non-numbers
    total += n

x = value otherwise (return 1) + 2                          # error: an exit must be the
                                                            #   whole right operand

When the left side is optional, the binding gets the unwrapped T. This is the one form that also allows a refutable pattern in a binding, because the failure case has somewhere to go:

fn radius_of(shape)
    Circle(r) = shape otherwise return 0.0
    r

With a fallible left side, otherwise return … (or break/continue) throws the error away — the reason for the failure is lost. That is sometimes exactly right (skip a malformed line); when the reason matters, propagate it instead with .context("…")? (§8.4). There is no guard keyword: x = … otherwise return is the guard.

3.8.3 Comparison chaining

Comparisons can be chained and read like mathematics:

if 0 <= index < items.len()
    print(items[index])

There is no ambiguity with explicit type arguments: those are written only after a capitalised type name and a dot (Channel.new<Int>(capacity: 10), §11.4), so a.b < c > (d) with a lowercase receiver is always a chained comparison.

a < b < c means a < b and b < c, with b evaluated once.

3.8.4 Arithmetic

  • Int arithmetic is checked: overflow stops the program with a clear error. Wrapping and saturating arithmetic are available as methods (a.wrapping_add(b), a.saturating_mul(b)).
  • / on two Ints divides and truncates toward zero; % is the matching remainder. Dividing an Int by zero stops the program. a.checked_div(b) returns Int?.
  • / on Floats follows IEEE 754.
  • There are no implicit numeric conversions: write n.to_float() or x.round().to_int().
  • a ** b raises a to the power b. It is right-associative (2 ** 3 ** 2 is 2 ** 9) and binds tighter than unary minus, so -2 ** 2 is -4, as in mathematics. On Int it is overflow-checked, and the exponent must not be negative: 2 ** -1 is a compile-time error (use 2.0 ** -1.0), and a negative Int exponent computed at run time panics.

3.9 Statements and expressions

Most constructs are expressions: if … then … else …, block if/else, match, blocks, and calls all produce values. Declarations (bindings, fn, type, trait, impl, import, test) and assignments are statements. The value of a block is the value of its last expression.

Bindings and assignment

There is no let. A name is introduced by writing it, and mut marks a name that can change:

total = 0                      # a new immutable binding
mut count = 0                  # a new mutable binding
count = count + 1              # `count` exists and is `mut`: reassignment
count += 1                     # the same
n: Int = 5                     # with a type annotation
mut ratio: Float = 0.0
(low, high) = bounds           # destructuring (§7.7)
Circle(r) = shape otherwise return 0.0   # refutable: only with `otherwise` (§3.8.2)

The rule for name = expr depends only on what is already visible:

name is… name = expr means
not yet bound in this function a new immutable binding
a visible mut binding reassignment
a visible immutable binding or immutable parameter a compile-time error: "total is immutable; write mut total = … where it is declared, or pick a new name"

mut name = expr always declares a new mutable binding. In a pattern, a name starting with an uppercase letter is a constructor or variant and a lowercase name is a new binding (§3.5), so Circle(r) = shape destructures and never calls anything. A refutable pattern (one that might not match) is allowed only with otherwise return/break/continue; without it, it is a compile-time error.

Destructuring always creates new bindings. Every lowercase name in a pattern on the left of = is a new binding, so a name that already exists is an error ("x already exists; a pattern always binds new names — to change x, declare it mut and assign it on its own"). The one exception is a parallel assignment: a tuple made only of visible mut names assigns them all at once, with the right side fully evaluated first, so (a, b) = (b, a) swaps. Mixing new and existing names in one tuple is an error.

mut a = 1
mut b = 2
(a, b) = (b, a)                # parallel assignment: a == 2, b == 1
(a, c) = (3, 4)                # error: `a` exists but `c` is new; do not mix

No shadowing. The rule is: you cannot bind a name that is currently visible, where visible means locals only: parameters, earlier bindings, and loop, pattern and lambda names in scope. Parameters (of functions and of lambdas), for loop variables, pattern bindings in match arms and if … is, and with … as names all count: each lives in its own block, but it may not reuse a name that is already visible there. A name bound before a block cannot be bound again inside it; a name bound inside a block may be bound again after that block ends, because the inner one is out of scope. Sibling blocks — the branches of one if/else or match, or two separate loops — may reuse a name, because neither can see the other:

fn report(items)
    count = items.len()
    for item in items
        count = item.size          # error: `count` is visible here (immutable)
        size = item.size           # fine: new inside the loop
    size = 0                       # fine: the loop's `size` is out of scope
    items.map(count -> count + 1)  # error: lambda parameter reuses `count`

Without let, a second x = … would otherwise be impossible to tell apart from an assignment, so Verse does not allow it at all; a transformed value gets a new name (raw = read_text(path)? then text = raw.trim()). Entry-file top-level bindings follow the script-local rules of §12.4.

Names from outside the function are not locals. A local may hide a prelude name silently (input = lines[0], error = e.message()) and may hide a module constant or an imported name (time = elapsed.seconds() after import std.time). Hiding an imported name warns only when the same function also uses that import — an actual collision ("fs hides the import std.fs, which this function also uses"). The same holds one level up: a file-level import hides a prelude name of the same spelling, so after import info, error from std.log the name error means std.log's function in that file, and the prelude error is not reachable there (there is no qualifier for prelude names; import std.log as a module, log.error(…), to keep both). Because this changes a name for the whole file, it warns on the import line: "error hides the prelude error". Names bound by with … as follow the same rule as other bindings: on a lock guard, the bound value can be changed only when written as mut value (§11.4).

A mut parameter is the caller's place under an exclusive borrow, so assigning to it replaces the caller's value in place (§5.3):

fn reset(mut list)
    list = []                      # the caller's list is now empty

There is still one form, x = …, for both meanings, so tools carry the difference: editors and verse fmt --check tooling must render a reassignment distinctly from a new binding (for example an inlay hint "reassign" before the name). This is a tooling requirement, not syntax.

Two warnings catch the usual slips:

  • an unused binding warns (prefix the name with _ to keep it on purpose); it is a warning only, and illustrative snippets in this document are exempt — the spec's examples are not compiled with warnings-as-errors;
  • a new binding whose name is one edit away from a visible mut binding warns, because it is probably a typo for an assignment:
warning: new binding `totl` looks like the mutable `total`
  --> sum.vs:6:5
   |
 2 |     mut total = 0
   |         ----- `total` is declared here
 6 |     totl = total + n
   |     ^^^^ this creates a new name
   |
help: did you mean to reassign `total`?   total = total + n

4. Types

4.1 Built-in scalar types

Type Description Examples
Int 64-bit signed integer, overflow-checked 0, -12, 1_000
Float 64-bit IEEE 754 floating point 3.14, 1e-9
Bool truth value true, false
Char one Unicode scalar value 'a', '\u{263A}'
Text immutable UTF-8 string "hello"
Bytes immutable sequence of bytes b"\x00\xFF"
Nothing the type of "no useful value" (result of print)

Sized numeric types (Int8 … Int64, UInt8 … UInt64, Float32) and arbitrary-precision BigInt and Decimal are provided by std.num for code that needs them.

Text is indexed by characters, not bytes: "héllo".len() is 5. Because positions count characters, indexing or slicing a Text by position (text[i], text[2..5]) may take time proportional to the length of the text. For the raw bytes, text.bytes() gives a read-only view of the UTF-8 bytes with constant-time indexing: "héllo".bytes().len() is 6, and text.bytes()[i] is the i-th byte as an Int from 0 to 255. It follows the rules for views (§9.3): it can be read, passed and bound to a name, but not stored or returned; .copy() gives an owned Bytes.

4.2 Type annotations and inference

Verse is statically typed, but types are visually optional: annotations may be left out almost everywhere — on local bindings, on function parameters, and on return types. The compiler infers them, checks everything at compile time, and never guesses: when it cannot decide, it stops and asks for one annotation at that exact spot.

count = 0                           # Int
ratio = 0.5                         # Float
ratio2: Float = 1                   # error: 1 is an Int; write 1.0
mut tags = []                       # element type decided by later use…
tags.push("new")                    # …so tags is List<Text>

fn greet(name)                      # inferred: any `name` that is Show; returns Text
    "Hello, {name}!"

fn greet_typed(name: Text): Text    # the same function, spelled out
    "Hello, {name}!"

fn double(n)                        # numeric; Int unless a caller says otherwise
    n * 2

Both styles are equally checked. Annotate where it helps a reader — at important boundaries, in teaching code, or to narrow a function on purpose — and leave the rest to the compiler.

Inference rules

  1. Unannotated parameters are implicit generics. Each one gets exactly the constraints its body needs, and nothing more:
  2. trait constraints from operations — interpolation or print gives Show, + gives Add, == gives Eq, < gives Order, for gives Iterable, indexing x[i] gives Index, .copy() gives Copyable, calling a trait method gives that trait;
  3. callable from calls — f(x) on a parameter f makes it a function type with matching parameters;
  4. structural constraints from field access and inherent method calls — person.name gives "has a field name", text.trim() gives "has a method trim()";
  5. a variant pattern (Circle(r) -> …) or passing the parameter to an annotated parameter fixes or narrows the type.

Every call site is checked against those constraints at compile time, and the compiler generates specialized code for each concrete type used — but the ownership check runs once, at the definition (rule 9), so whether a body compiles never depends on which types its callers use. So greet(42), greet("Ana") and greet(ana) all work if the argument is Show, while greet(some_function) is a compile error at the call site. Structural constraints are inferred only; they cannot be written by hand in 0.1. To narrow a function on purpose, annotate a concrete type (person: Person). 2. Numeric literals default to Int and Float. fn double(n) with n * 2 accepts any numeric type; where nothing else decides (for example x = double(3)), the literal makes it Int, and double(2.5) is a Float. 3. Recursion needs an annotation. A function that calls itself, directly or through other functions, must annotate its parameters and return type; otherwise the compiler reports an ambiguity at the recursive call. 4. When inference cannot decide, it says so — exactly there. The error names the spot, says which annotation to add, and lists the constraints it did infer:

error: cannot infer the element type of this list --> stats.vs:2:5 | 1 | fn empty_scores() | - add a return type here, for example `: List<Int>` 2 | [] | ^^ a List of something, but nothing says of what

  1. Fallible return types are inferred from ?. A function whose body uses ? on fallible values (or returns an error(…)) gets a fallible return type made of its success type and the errors that can escape, normalized as in §4.6. A fn load(path) whose body is text = read_text(path)? followed by text.trim() returns Text | Error. A ? on an optional gives an optional return type.
  2. Inferred types are visible on demand. Editors (through verse lsp) show inferred parameter and return types as inline hints. verse fmt never inserts or removes annotations.
  3. Record fields keep their annotations unless a default value implies the type (active = true is a Bool field; tags: List<Text> = [] still needs its annotation because [] says nothing about the elements).
  4. mut and take are always written. How a function treats its argument (borrow, exclusive mut borrow, or take) is never inferred (§5.3).
  5. Ownership is checked once, at the definition. Inside a generic or unannotated function, every parameter type that is unannotated or generic is treated as an opaque, non-Copy type, unless a Copy bound says otherwise (<T: Copy>). One bound is inferred instead of rejected, so that simple getters need no annotation: an unannotated function that returns a field, element or lookup read through a borrowed parameter gets an inferred Copy bound on the returned type, recorded in verse.api like any other inferred constraint:

``verse fn age_of(person) person.age # fine: inferred bound "person.age` is Copy"

fn first_name(person) person.name # fine here too: inferred bound "person.name is Copy"

first_name(ana) # error at the call site: first_name returns # person.name by value, so the field must be # Copy, and Person.name is Text # help: return person.name.copy(), or take # the parameter with take ```

Errors about a function's body appear at the definition. The only call-site errors are unmet bounds, written or inferred, and they name the bound. Because the check never looks at callers, verse.api is enough to check other modules (§12.3).

Inference and module boundaries

Inference never crosses a module boundary. Exported functions may have inferred signatures only because every package commits a generated interface file, verse.api, that records each exported signature as the compiler inferred it. Other modules are type-checked against verse.api, never against another module's body, and the build fails if an inferred exported signature drifts from the recorded one until someone runs verse api update on purpose. A body edit therefore cannot silently change the public API. See §12.3 and §16.4.

4.3 Record types

A record type groups named fields. Fields are listed on indented lines.

type User
    name: Text
    age: Int
    email: Text? = none
    roles: List<Text> = []
    active = true                 # type implied by the default: Bool

Fields keep their type annotations unless a default value implies the type (§4.2). Fields may have default values. Construct a record by calling the type name with named arguments; positional arguments are allowed in field order. When a variable has the same name as the field, the value may be left out — User(name:, age:) means User(name: name, age: age). This field punning works the same way in construction and in patterns (§7.3).

ana = User(name: "Ana", age: 30)
bruno = User("Bruno", 17)
name = "Carla"
age = 41
carla = User(name:, age:)
print(ana.name)

Fields are visible inside the module that defines the type. To make a field visible to other modules, mark it export (§12.3).

Copies

Every value has one owner (§4.9). copy() with no arguments makes an independent duplicate; the same method with named arguments makes a duplicate with some fields changed:

twin = ana.copy()                 # an independent User
older = ana.copy(age: 31)         # ana is unchanged

.copy() is the one way to duplicate a value, with or without changes. It is provided by the built-in trait Copyable (§10.4), which almost every type has automatically; the exceptions are Task<T>, types that implement Cleanup (files, locks, temporary directories), and anything that contains them.

4.4 Variant types

A variant type (also called a sum type or tagged union) is one of several named alternatives, each with its own fields.

type Shape = Circle(radius: Float) | Square(side: Float)

type Direction = North | East | South | West

type Json = Null
    | Flag(value: Bool)
    | Number(value: Float)
    | Str(value: Text)
    | Array(items: List<Json>)
    | Object(fields: Map<Text, Json>)

Long variant lists may continue across lines when each line starts with | (§3.4). A type X = header never opens a field block.

A variant name may not collide with a type that is already in scope (Int, Float, Text, Error, an imported type, …). This one rule keeps type and alias apart:

type Direction = North | East | South | West   # fine: four new unit variants
type Meters = Float            # error: `Float` is an existing type
                               #   help: to give it another name, write `alias Meters = Float`
type Value = Int | Text        # error: help: write `alias Value = Int | Text`
type Reply = Text(body: Text) | Empty   # error: variant name `Text` is already a type

Variants are constructed like records — Circle(radius: 2.0) or Circle(2.0) — and may be qualified with the type name when a name is ambiguous: Shape.Circle(2.0). Variant types may be recursive; the compiler handles the indirection.

4.5 Tuples

A tuple groups a fixed number of values of possibly different types.

pair = (3, "three")                 # (Int, Text)
print(pair.0)                       # 3
(number, word) = pair               # destructuring

Tuple elements may optionally be labeled, in which case they can be read by name as well as by position:

fn divide(a: Int, b: Int): (quotient: Int, remainder: Int)
    (quotient: a / b, remainder: a % b)

result = divide(17, 5)
print("{result.quotient} remainder {result.remainder}")   # 3 remainder 2
(q, r) = result

4.6 Optional, union and fallible types

  • T? is an optional: a T or none.
  • A | B is a union: a value that is either an A or a B. The member types must be distinct.
  • A union with a member that implements the Error trait is fallible: Int | Error is "an Int, or an error". Members implementing Error form the error side; the others form the success side.

? binds tighter than | in types: Text? | Error is "an optional text, or an error". Optionals nest: Int?? is a different type from Int? (§8.1).

Union normalization. Unions are flattened and de-duplicated ((A | B) | A is A | B), and a specific error type in a union that also contains Error is absorbed by Error: Text | FetchError | Error normalizes to Text | Error. Once a value has been widened to Error, ? cannot narrow it back to FetchError; use a typed pattern in match (err: FetchError -> …) to inspect the concrete error.

Both are covered in depth in §8.

4.7 Function types

The type of a function is written fn(ParamTypes): Ret:

double: fn(Int): Int = n -> n * 2
fn apply_twice(f: fn(Int): Int, x: Int): Int
    f(f(x))

4.8 Type aliases

An alias gives an existing type a second, shorter name. It does not create a new type; the two names are interchangeable.

alias Headers = Map<Text, Text>
alias Handler = fn(Request): Response | Error
alias Loaded = Config | Error

alias is required to name a union of existing types. In a type declaration, | always introduces new variants (§4.4), so type X = A | B and alias X = A | B can never be confused.

To create a genuinely distinct type (so that a UserId cannot be mixed up with an ordinary Int), declare a one-field record:

type UserId
    value: Int

4.9 Ownership, moves and copies

Every value has exactly one owner: a binding, a field of a record, an element of a collection, or a task. When the owner's scope ends, the value is freed — immediately and deterministically.

Copy types. Scalars (Int, Float, Bool, Char, Nothing) and records, variants and tuples made only of copy types (a Point(x: Float, y: Float), a Shape, an (Int, Int)) are copied implicitly whenever they are assigned or passed. There is no size limit: whether a type is Copy depends only on the kinds of its fields, never on its size. A copy is never inserted silently except for Copy types and literals (§3.8.2), and moves happen at a value's last use; adding a non-Copy field (say a Text) to an all-scalar record makes it non-Copy, and the compiler then reports every place that relied on the implicit copy. Everything else — Text, Bytes, collections, and records that contain them — is moved when it gets a new owner. A non-Copy value is never duplicated implicitly; anywhere an implicit duplicate would be needed, the compiler asks for .copy().

Moves. A value moves when it is:

  • bound with mut b = a, or with b = a when a is not used afterwards;
  • stored in a field or a collection (record construction, push, map[k] = v);
  • returned from a function;
  • passed to a take parameter (§5.3) or into a task with spawn (§11.1);
  • captured by an escaping lambda (§5.4).

When b = a appears and a is used afterwards, nothing moves: b is a read-only local view of a (a borrow, §5.3), and a cannot be changed while b is in use. A binding to a collection chain is a local view in the same way (§9.5).

Moving a field out. Moving a field out of an owned value at the value's last use is allowed: the field gets its new owner and the rest of the value is freed. If the value is used afterwards (or is only borrowed), moving the field is the usual move error, with a .copy() suggestion:

fn body_of(url)
    response = get(url)?
    response.body             # fine: `response` is owned and not used again

Moves are tracked per control-flow path. A value moved in one branch of an if or match counts as moved after it on that path, and a value moved inside a loop counts as moved on the next iteration.

mut a = [1, 2, 3]
mut b = a.copy()              # an independent list
b.push(4)
print(a)                      # [1, 2, 3]
print(b)                      # [1, 2, 3, 4]

names = ["Ana", "Bruno"]
mut roster = names            # moves: `names` is not used afterwards
roster.push("Carla")

p = Point(x: 1.0, y: 2.0)     # an all-Float record: copied implicitly
q = p
print(p.x + q.x)              # fine: q is a copy

Using a moved value is a compile-time error that says where the move happened and suggests .copy():

mut inbox: List<Text> = []
note = "remember the milk"
inbox.push(note)
print(note)

error: `note` is used after it was moved
  --> notes.vs:4:7
   |
 3 | inbox.push(note)
   |            ---- `note` moved into `inbox` here
 4 | print(note)
   |       ^^^^ used here after the move
   |
help: to keep using `note`, store a copy:   inbox.push(note.copy())

Errors name the later use. Whether b = a, a for loop variable (§6.3), a pattern binding (§7.7) or a chain result (§9.5) owns its value or only views it depends on whether the source is used later. So adding a line below can turn working code into an error. Every error caused by such a flip must name the later use that kept the source alive:

error: `person` is only a view, so it cannot be stored in `adults`
  --> people.vs:8:16
   |
 7 | for person in people
   |     ------ `person` is a view because `people` is used again on line 12
 8 |     adults.push(person)
   |                 ^^^^^^ stored here
...
12 | print(people.len())
   |       ------ the later use that keeps `people` alive
   |
help: write `person.copy()`, or move the use on line 12 above the loop

Inside a loop, the error points at both the move and the later use — which is the same line, one iteration later:

greeting = "hi"
mut all: List<Text> = []
for name in names
    all.push(greeting)        # error: `greeting` moved here in one iteration
                              #   and used again here in the next
                              #   help: all.push(greeting.copy())

Mutability is a property of the binding, and it is deep. mut means "can change" everywhere it appears — on a binding, a parameter (§5.3) or self (§5.6):

  • A plain binding (user = …) can never be reassigned, and the value it owns can never be changed — not its fields, not its elements.
  • A mut binding (mut guest = …) can be reassigned with guest = …, and its fields and elements can be changed in place. Reassigning frees the old value first.

Because there is no let and no shadowing (§3.9), guest = … on an existing name is always a reassignment, and on an immutable name always an error.

user = User(name: "Ana", age: 30)
user.age = 31                     # error: `user` is immutable; write
                                  #   `mut user = …` where it is declared

mut guest = User(name: "Guest", age: 0)
guest.age = 18                    # fine
guest = User(name: "Other", age: 5)   # fine; the old guest is freed

Methods that change their receiver declare mut self and can only be called on mutable bindings (§5.6).

Order inside an assignment. In place = value (and place += value), the right side is evaluated completely before the place, so a value can be read on the right and moved into the place on the left in the same statement. The receiver and index expressions on the left are evaluated after the right side, left to right among themselves; everything else is evaluated left to right:

counts[word] = counts.get(word, default: 0) + 1   # borrows `word`, then moves it

4.10 Memory model

Verse has no garbage collector and no manual memory management:

  1. Single ownership. Every value has one owner and is freed at the end of its owner's scope (or when a mut owner is reassigned). There is no collector running in the background and no pause.
  2. No references in the surface language. There are no pointer types, no reference types, and no lifetime syntax. Functions borrow their arguments, but borrows are second-class: they cannot be stored in a field, returned, or sent to another task (§5.3). This is what lets the compiler prove, without annotations, that nothing is ever used after it is freed.
  3. Recursive types are boxed for you. Variant types such as Json or Tree<T> are stored with the indirection they need; the boxes are owned like any other value and freed with their owner.
  4. Cleanup is deterministic. A type that implements Cleanup has its cleanup(mut self) run automatically when its owner's scope ends — also during a panic (§13).
  5. Sharing is opt-in. The only ways for two owners to share one value are the handle types Shared<T> (shared read-only), Guarded<T> (shared, mutable behind a lock), Weak<Shared<T>> / Weak<Guarded<T>> (non-owning), and the channel sender Sender<T> (§11.4). Copying a handle is cheap and shares the value behind it; the copy must be written explicitly as .copy(), like every other copy (a Task<T> and a Receiver<T> are never shared: they cannot be copied, and they move; wait takes a task).

Consequences:

  • No use-after-free, no double free, no dangling reference, and no data race, in any program that compiles.
  • Cycles are possible only through Shared/Guarded handles (for example two Guarded nodes pointing at each other). Such a cycle is never freed; use a Weak<Shared<T>> or Weak<Guarded<T>> for back-pointers to avoid it.
  • Arbitrary graphs (trees with parent links, graphs with cycles) are built either with Shared/Weak handles or — usually simpler and faster — with an index-based arena: store the nodes in a List<Node> and refer to them by Int index.
type Node
    name: Text
    children: List<Int> = []      # indices into the arena
    parent: Int? = none

type Tree
    nodes: List<Node> = []

impl Tree
    fn add(mut self, take name, parent: Int?): Int
        self.nodes.push(Node(name:, parent:))
        if parent is p?
            # The argument is evaluated first, then the `mut` borrow of the
            # receiver begins (§5.3), so reading `self.nodes` here is fine.
            self.nodes[p].children.push(self.nodes.len() - 1)
        self.nodes.len() - 1

The trade-offs of this model are discussed honestly in §18.10.

5. Functions

5.1 Declaring functions

A function is declared with fn, its parameters, an optional return type after a colon, and an indented body. The last expression of the body is the return value. Parameter and return types may be written or left to inference (§4.2):

fn greet(name)
    "Hello, {name}!"

fn hypotenuse(a: Float, b: Float): Float
    squares = a * a + b * b
    squares.sqrt()

A function whose body ends in a statement (or that is annotated without a return type and never returns a value) returns Nothing:

fn log(message)
    print("[log] {message}")

5.2 Early return

return exits a function early. It is needed only when leaving before the last line:

fn classify(n)
    if n < 0
        return "negative"
    if n == 0
        return "zero"
    "positive"

Two compact forms exist for the most common early exits. A postfix guard puts the condition after the exit (§6.7), and otherwise return unwraps an optional or leaves (§3.8.2):

fn describe_user(id)
    return "invalid id" if id <= 0
    user = find_user(id) otherwise return "no such user"
    "{user.name}, {user.age}"

5.3 Parameters and arguments

Borrow, mut, and take

How a function receives each argument is part of its signature and is always written explicitly (it is never inferred):

Parameter Meaning Call site
p read-only borrow (the default): the function may look, not change or keep f(x)
mut p exclusive mutable borrow: the function may change the caller's value in place f(mut x) — x must be a mut binding
take p consume: the function becomes the owner; the caller's value moves (copy types are copied) f(x) — no marker; the move is visible because x must not be used afterwards

mut means "can change" in every position: a mut binding can be reassigned and changed in place (§3.9, §4.9), a mut parameter may change the caller's value, and a mut self method may change its receiver (§5.6). Parameter names count as bindings of the function, so a body cannot bind a parameter's name again (§3.9). A mut parameter is the caller's place under an exclusive borrow, so assigning to it replaces the caller's value in place:

fn reset(mut list)
    list = []                           # the caller's list is now empty

mut names = ["Ana", "Bruno"]
reset(mut names)                        # names == []

type Cart
    items: List<Item> = []

fn total(cart)                          # borrows `cart`
    cart.items.map(.price).sum()

fn add_item(mut cart, take item)        # changes `cart`, keeps `item`
    cart.items.push(item)

mut cart = Cart()
apple = Item(name: "apple", price: 0.5)
add_item(mut cart, apple)               # `mut` at the call site; `apple` moves
print(total(cart))
print(apple.name)                       # error: `apple` was moved into `add_item`
                                        #   help: add_item(mut cart, apple.copy())

The mut marker is written at the call site of a plain function, so a reader can see which arguments may change. Method calls (cart.add(item)) do not carry it (§5.6). A value cannot be passed as mut and also as another argument of the same call (merge(mut a, a) is an error), so a function with a mut parameter always has exclusive access.

Arguments first, then the exclusive borrow. All arguments of a call are evaluated first, left to right; only then does the exclusive borrow for mut parameters (and for a mut self receiver, §5.6) begin. So an argument may read the value that is about to be borrowed mutably — the same idea as the assignment rule in §4.9:

add_item(mut cart, Item(name: "extra", price: total(cart)))   # fine
history.push(history.len())                                   # fine

Borrows are second-class

A borrowed parameter is a view of the caller's value for the duration of the call. It cannot be stored in a field or collection, cannot be returned, and cannot be sent to another task. In particular, a function cannot return a reference into its argument — it returns a copy, an owned value, or an optional:

fn first_name(person: Person)
    person.name                  # error: cannot return a borrow of `person`
                                 #   (`name` is `Text`, not Copy)
                                 #   help: return a copy: person.name.copy()

fn first_name(person: Person)
    person.name.copy()           # fine: the caller owns the result

fn age_of(person)
    person.age                   # fine: a copy, with an inferred `Copy` bound

An unannotated getter such as age_of compiles with an inferred Copy bound on the returned field (§4.2, rule 9). Errors about a function's body appear at the definition. The only call-site errors are unmet bounds, written or inferred, and they name the bound.

This is the price of having no lifetimes: there is no lifetime syntax and no elision rules to learn, because a borrow can never outlive the call that created it. The cost, stated plainly: accessor-style functions copy, and code that would return a view into a large structure in Rust or C++ is written differently in Verse — it changes the structure in place through mut, takes ownership with take, returns an index, or shares the data through Shared<T> (§11.4).

Default values and named arguments

Parameters may have default values. At the call site, arguments can be passed by position or by name. Positional arguments come first; once a named argument appears, the rest must be named.

fn connect(host, port = 80, secure = false)
    ...

connect("a.com")
connect("a.com", port: 443, secure: true)
connect("a.com", secure: true)              # port uses its default
connect(host: "a.com", port: 8080)

A named argument is written name: value — the same shape as a map entry ({"name": value}) or a record field. When the value is a variable with the same name as the parameter, it can be left out: connect(host:, port:) means connect(host: host, port: port) (punning, the same shorthand as in record construction and patterns). Default values are evaluated at each call, never shared between calls, and a default fixes the parameter's type when nothing else does (port = 80 makes port an Int). Named arguments are especially encouraged for Bool parameters, and verse fmt --check warns on positional true/false arguments.

5.4 Lambdas

A lambda is written param -> expression. Multiple parameters are wrapped in parentheses; types are inferred from context but may be written.

double = n -> n * 2
add = (a, b) -> a + b
shout = (text: Text) -> text.upper() + "!"
greet_all = () -> print("Hello, everyone")

Multi-line lambdas: the closing rule

When a line inside an open ( ends with ->, the lambda's body is the indented block that follows, and the dedent that ends the block also closes the parenthesis opened on that line. The lambda must be the last argument of that call:

labels = orders.map(order ->
    status = if order.paid then "paid" else "due"
    due = order.due_date.format("%d %b")
    "{order.id}: {status} (due {due})"
print(labels.join("\n"))

There is no separate "trailing lambda" syntax: a lambda is always an argument inside the call's parentheses, and the closing rule only saves writing the lonely ). In detail:

  • One dedent closes every parenthesis opened by block lambdas on the lines it ends (for example a block lambda nested inside another).
  • Nothing can follow the closed call on the dedent line, so a call cannot be chained after it; bind the result first (labels = orders.map(order -> … then labels.sum()).
  • Writing the ) explicitly on its own line is accepted; verse fmt removes it (§16.1).

Lambdas in match arms

-> is used only by lambdas and match arms, so a lambda that forms the body of a match arm must be wrapped in parentheses to keep the two arrows apart:

fn operation(op: Op): fn(Int): Int
    match op
        Double -> (n -> n * 2)
        Negate -> (n -> -n)

Lambdas that appear as call arguments are already inside parentheses and need nothing extra: Evens -> items.filter(n -> n % 2 == 0).

Key-path shorthand

A leading dot that starts an expression — right after (, , or an operator — is a one-parameter lambda that reads from its argument:

ages = users.map(.age)                      # same as u -> u.age
names = users.map(.name.copy())             # u -> u.name.copy()  (owned results, §9.5)
loud = users.map(.name.upper())             # u -> u.name.upper()
firsts = pairs.map(.0)                      # p -> p.0
by_age = users.sort_by(.age)

Only plain access chains (fields, tuple positions, method calls) are allowed after the dot. Anything with an operator is a compile error that suggests a lambda: users.filter(.age >= 18) → write users.filter(u -> u.age >= 18). After a complete expression, a leading dot still continues a method chain (§3.4). There are no leading-dot variant names (.north is not North).

Captures: borrowed or moved

A lambda uses variables from its surroundings in one of two ways, decided by what happens to the lambda:

  • A lambda that is only called while the function it was passed to runs (map, filter, sort_by, any, each, …) borrows its captures read-only. So items.map(x -> x + offset) does not consume offset, and people.filter(p -> p.city == city) leaves city usable. A function-typed parameter is non-escaping in this sense unless it is declared take.
  • An escaping lambda — returned, stored in a field or collection, passed to a take parameter, or used in spawn — moves its captures (copy types are copied). Using a captured value after the lambda escaped is the usual use-after-move error, with a .copy() suggestion.

A lambda cannot reassign a captured mut variable; use a fold, a loop, or a returned value instead.

fn make_greeter(greeting)                   # returns an escaping lambda
    words = greeting.copy()                 # the lambda needs its own copy
    name -> "{words}, {name}!"

hello = make_greeter("Hello")
print(hello("Ana"))

Named functions are values too: shapes.map(area) passes the function area.

Tuple auto-spread

A lambda (or function) with N parameters may be called with a single N-tuple; the tuple is spread across the parameters. This is what makes two-parameter lambdas work with zip, enumerate and entries, which produce pairs:

totals = prices.zip(quantities).map((price, qty) -> price * qty)
lines = names.enumerate().map((i, name) -> "{i + 1}. {name}")
report = ages.entries().map((name, age) -> "{name} is {age}")

Spreading happens only when the arity matches exactly; a one-parameter lambda receives the whole tuple (pair -> pair.0).

? inside a lambda

? inside a lambda returns from the lambda, not from the enclosing function, so the lambda's own return type becomes fallible (see §8.3):

doubled = inputs.map(text -> text.trim().to_int()? * 2)       # List<Int | ParseError>

5.5 Generic functions

Every unannotated parameter is already an implicit generic (§4.2). Explicit generic parameters name the type so it can be used in several places:

fn first<T: Copyable>(items: List<T>): T?
    items.get(0).copy()           # `.copy()` on the optional: an owned `T?`

The Copyable bound is what allows .copy() on a T (§10.4): the ownership check runs once, at the definition, and treats T as an opaque, non-Copy type unless a bound says otherwise (§4.2, rule 9). Without the bound, items.get(0).copy() is a compile error that suggests adding T: Copyable.

See §10.

5.6 Methods

Methods are functions declared inside an impl block for a type. The first parameter is self.

type Dog
    name: Text
    tricks: List<Text> = []

impl Dog
    fn speak(self)
        "{self.name} says woof"

    fn learn(mut self, take trick)
        self.tricks.push(trick)

    ## A constructor-style function with no `self`.
    fn puppy(take name)
        Dog(name:)

mut rex = Dog.puppy("Rex")
rex.learn("sit")
print(rex.speak())
  • self borrows the receiver read-only.
  • mut self borrows it exclusively and may change it — including assigning its fields directly, as in self.name = new_name or self.age += 1. As with mut parameters, the arguments are evaluated first and only then does the exclusive borrow of the receiver begin (§5.3), so self.nodes[p].children.push(self.nodes.len() - 1) is fine.
  • take self consumes the receiver (for example task.wait()); the receiver moves, so it must not be used afterwards.
  • Method calls look the same whether or not they mutate — cart.add(item) carries no mut marker, deliberately: the receiver is the dotted name in front, so it is already visible. Instead, the receiver of a mut self method must be a mut binding (or a mutable field/element of one); calling it on an immutable binding is a compile-time error that names the binding.
  • A function in an impl block without self is an associated function, called as Type.name(...).
  • Self inside an impl names the type being implemented.

A type can have several impl blocks, in the same module as the type.

5.7 Uniform call syntax

Any function in scope can also be called with dot syntax, x.f(y), when its first parameter accepts x. Then x.f(y) means f(x, y):

fn shout(text: Text)
    text.upper() + "!"

print("hello".shout())                 # same as shout("hello")

report = orders.filter(o -> o.paid).total_by_customer().format_table()
  • A method always wins. If the type of x has a method f (inherent or from a trait in scope), x.f(y) calls the method.
  • Ambiguity is an error. If two functions in scope could both be called as x.f(…), the call is a compile-time error that lists both and asks you to call one as module.f(x, …).
  • Parameter modes carry over: if the first parameter is mut, the receiver must be a mut binding (and, as with methods, no marker is written); if it is take, the receiver moves.

Uniform call syntax is how Verse spells left-to-right pipelines; there is no separate |> operator.

6. Control flow

6.1 if / else

if balance < 0
    print("Overdrawn")
else if balance == 0
    print("Empty")
else
    print("In credit")

A block always starts on the line after its header — there is no colon at the end of if balance < 0. Conditions must have type Bool; there is no truthiness.

One-line form: if … then … else …

When choosing between two values, use the one-line expression form. Both branches are required, and each is a single expression:

label = if count == 1 then "item" else "items"
sign = if n < 0 then -1 else if n == 0 then 0 else 1
print("{count} {if count == 1 then "item" else "items"}")

The block form is also an expression when it has an else and each branch ends in a value:

greeting = if hour < 12
    part = "morning"
    "Good {part}"
else
    "Hello"

then appears only in the one-line form; else appears only with if.

When an if (either form) or a match produces a value, its result is a view only if every branch is a view or a literal; otherwise it is owned and each view branch needs .copy() — the same rule as otherwise (§3.8.2).

6.2 if … is — testing a pattern

To run a block only when a value has a certain shape, test it with is (§7.6). The names bound by the pattern are available inside the block. The pattern user? matches a present optional and binds the value inside it:

if find_user(id) is user?
    print("Found {user.name}")
else
    print("No such user")

if shape is Circle(r)
    print("A circle of radius {r}")

There is no separate pattern-binding form of if; is is the one way to branch on a pattern.

6.3 for loops

for iterates over anything that implements the Iterable trait: lists, sets, maps, ranges, text (characters), channel receivers, and more.

for name in ["Ana", "Bruno", "Carla"]
    print("Hi, {name}")

for i in 0..3
    print(i)                       # 0, 1, 2

for (word, count) in word_counts   # maps yield (key: K, value: V) pairs
    print("{word}: {count}")

for (index, item) in items.enumerate()
    print("{index + 1}. {item}")

The loop variable is a fresh immutable binding on every iteration. Patterns may be used to destructure (§7).

Ownership in loops. for x in items borrows each element while items is still used after the loop. When the loop is the collection's last use, the loop takes the collection and each x is owned, so it can be moved elsewhere without a copy:

mut adults: List<Person> = []
for person in people                 # last use of `people`: each person is owned
    if person.age >= 18
        adults.push(person)          # moves the person; no copy needed

6.4 Ranges

Range Contains
1..10 1, 2, …, 9 (end excluded)
1..=10 1, 2, …, 10 (end included)
(1..10).step(2) 1, 3, 5, 7, 9
(1..=10).reverse() 10, 9, …, 1

Ranges are values of type Range<Int> (also Range<Char>), support in (if age in 13..=19), and can slice lists and text: items[1..3], name[0..=2].

Inside slice brackets only, either end may be left open:

Slice Meaning
items[2..] from index 2 to the end
items[..3] the first three elements (indices 0, 1, 2)
items[..=3] indices 0 through 3

Open-ended ranges are not values: r = 2.. and for i in 1.. are compile-time errors. Slicing past the end of a list panics, like indexing.

6.5 while, break, and continue

mut attempts = 0
while attempts < 3
    attempts += 1
    if try_connect()
        break
    print("Retrying…")

for line in lines
    continue if line.starts_with("#")     # postfix guard, §6.7
    process(line)

break leaves the innermost loop; continue skips to its next iteration. A loop may be given a label — written before the loop as label:, in the ": means is named" sense — when you need to leave or continue an outer loop:

outer: for row in grid
    for cell in row
        if cell == target
            break outer

continue outer works the same way. Labels may be placed on for and while loops only.

A while true loop with break is the idiom for an unbounded loop.

6.6 pass

pass is an explicit "do nothing" for blocks that must exist syntactically:

match event
    Click(x, y) -> handle_click(x, y)
    _ -> pass

6.7 Postfix guards

The three exits — return, break and continue — may be followed by if condition on the same line. The exit happens only when the condition is true:

fn safe_ratio(a, b)
    return 0.0 if b == 0.0
    a / b

for line in lines
    continue if line.is_empty()
    break if line == "END"
    process(line)

The rules are deliberately narrow: only return, break and continue take a postfix if; it fits on one line; there is no else; and there is no unless. Everything else uses an ordinary if block. The guard reads as a sentence ("continue if the line is empty") and keeps the main path of a loop or function unindented. For unwrapping an optional while exiting, use x = … otherwise return (§3.8.2). return, break or continue followed by if is always a guard; to return a conditional expression, parenthesize it: return (if c then a else b) (§3.8).

7. Pattern matching

7.1 match

match compares a value against patterns, top to bottom, and evaluates the arm of the first pattern that fits. Each arm is pattern -> expression, or pattern -> followed by an indented block.

type Shape = Circle(radius: Float) | Square(side: Float)

fn area(s: Shape): Float
    match s
        Circle(r) -> 3.14 * r * r
        Square(side) -> side * side

fn describe(s: Shape): Text
    match s
        Circle(r) ->
            size = if r > 10.0 then "large" else "small"
            "a {size} circle"
        Square(_) -> "a square"

match is an expression; all arms must produce compatible types. An arm whose body is a lambda must parenthesize it — Double -> (n -> n * 2) — because the first -> after a pattern always ends the pattern (see §5.4).

7.2 Exhaustiveness

The compiler checks that every possible value is handled. Forgetting a variant is a compile-time error that names the missing case:

error: match is not exhaustive
  --> shapes.vs:4:5
   |
 4 |     match s
   |     ^^^^^^^ missing case: Triangle(_, _, _)

Use _ to explicitly handle "everything else".

Unreachable arms. An arm whose pattern is a single lowercase name (or _) with no guard matches everything. If such an arm is not the last arm, every arm after it is reported as an unreachable arm error. This catches a common slip — writing north -> instead of North ->, which would otherwise bind a new variable and swallow every case:

error: unreachable arm
  --> compass.vs:5:9
   |
 4 |         north -> "up"
   |         ----- this arm matches every value (`north` is a new variable)
 5 |         South -> "down"
   |         ^^^^^ so this arm can never run
   |
help: did you mean the variant `North`?

Even in the last position, where a catch-all is legal, a binding whose name is the lowercase spelling of a variant of the matched type (north when North exists) gets a warning that suggests the variant or a different name.

7.3 Kinds of patterns

Pattern Matches Example
Literal an equal value 0, "quit", 'a', true
Binding anything, naming it x
Wildcard anything, discarding it _
Variant a variant, destructuring fields by position Circle(r)
Named fields a variant or record by field name User(name:, age: 18)
Tuple a tuple of matching parts (0, y)
List a list by shape [], [x], [first, ..rest]
Range a number or char within range 0..=9, 'a'..='z'
Alternatives any of several patterns "y" | "yes"
Typed a union member by type (top level only) n: Int, err: Error, _: Error
Present a present optional, binding its value user?, _?
none an absent optional none

Field patterns. Inside the parentheses of a variant or record pattern, name: pattern always means "the field name must match pattern", and name: alone is punning for name: name (bind the field to a variable of the same name). User(name:, age: 18) binds name and requires age to equal 18. Fields not mentioned are ignored.

Typed patterns (n: Int) are allowed only at the top level of an arm, to pick a member of a union. Inside parentheses, a typed binding is written as a field pattern whose pattern is itself typed: Reply(body: b: Text). This keeps User(age: Int) from having two readings — it can only mean "field age matches the pattern Int", which is rejected because Int is a type, not a variant.

Present patterns. p? matches an optional that is present and binds its value to p; _? matches any present value. Together with none they cover an optional exactly, and they nest: Person(email: e?) matches a person whose email is present and binds it to e.

fn summary(items: List<Int>): Text
    match items
        [] -> "empty"
        [x] -> "just {x}"
        [first, ..rest] -> "{first} and {rest.len()} more"

fn grade(score: Int): Char
    match score
        90..=100 -> 'A'
        80..90 -> 'B'
        70..80 -> 'C'
        _ -> 'F'

fn answer(input: Text): Bool
    match input.lower()
        "y" | "yes" -> true
        _ -> false

7.4 Guards

An arm may add a condition with if:

match point
    (0, 0) -> "origin"
    (x, y) if x == y -> "on the diagonal"
    (x, _) if x < 0 -> "left half"
    _ -> "somewhere else"

7.5 Matching optionals and fallibles

match find_user(id)
    none -> print("not found")
    user? -> print("hello, {user.name}")     # user: User

match parse_age(input)
    age: Int -> print("age is {age}")
    err: Error -> print("invalid: {err.message()}")

match person
    Person(email: e?) -> send_welcome(e)
    Person(name:, email: none) -> print("{name} has no email")

For a nested optional such as Int?? (§8.1), x?? matches a present inner value, none? matches "present but empty", and none matches the outer absence.

7.6 is — a pattern as a condition

value is Pattern is a Bool expression. When used as an if condition, the bindings in the pattern are available inside the block. This is the one way to branch on a pattern without a full match (there is no separate pattern-binding if):

if shape is Circle(r)
    print("radius {r}")

if settings["theme"] is theme?
    apply(theme)

circles = shapes.filter(s -> s is Circle(_))

Bindings from is are visible only in the if block, never in else or after the if. is used outside an if condition binds nothing.

7.7 Destructuring in bindings and for

Patterns that always match (irrefutable patterns) may be used on the left of a binding and in for. A pattern always binds new names; the one exception, a parallel assignment to a tuple of mut names such as (a, b) = (b, a), is described in §3.9:

(x, y) = position
User(name:, age:) = current_user
[head, ..tail] = items               # error: refutable; the list might be empty
for (key, value) in settings
    print("{key} = {value}")

A refutable pattern in a binding is a compile-time error; use match or if … is instead — or, when the failure case should leave the function or loop, the pattern = … otherwise return/break/continue form (§3.8.2):

[head, ..tail] = items otherwise return none

Ownership of bindings. Names bound by a pattern borrow from the matched value. If the matched value is owned and this is its last use, the bindings take ownership of the parts instead, so they can be moved on without copies.

7.8 match without a subject

When the choice depends on conditions rather than on the shape of one value, leave out the subject. Each arm is then a Bool condition, tried top to bottom:

fn sign_label(n)
    match
        n < 0 -> "negative"
        n == 0 -> "zero"
        _ -> "positive"

fee = match
    order.total > 100.0 -> 0.0
    order.express -> 15.0
    _ -> 5.0

A subject-less match is an expression, uses the ordinary arm syntax (including blocks after ->), and must end with a _ -> arm; without it the compiler reports "match is not exhaustive", because no set of conditions can be proved to cover every case. It replaces long if … else if … else chains that choose a value.

8. Errors and missing values

Verse has two related, but distinct, ideas:

  • Missing values — "there may be nothing here" — use optional types T?.
  • Errors — "something went wrong, and here is why" — use fallible types T | E.

Neither involves exceptions or null. Two forms of ?, one pattern and one word, otherwise, cover almost everything:

Form Where Meaning
T? type a value that may be missing
expr? postfix stop early: if expr is an error or missing, return it from the current function
x? pattern match a present value (§7.3)
a otherwise b expression fallback: a if usable, else b

A plain dot looks through an optional when the chain is consumed by one of these (§8.1); there is no separate safe-access operator.

8.1 Optional types T?

There is no null. A value of type T is always a real T. A value that might be absent has type T?, and is either a T or none.

fn find_user(id: Int): User?
    users.find(u -> u.id == id).copy()      # `users`: a module constant; `find`
                                            #   returns a view (§9.5), so copy it

maybe: Text? = none
present: Text? = "here"         # a T is automatically a T?

You cannot use a T? where a T is expected; the compiler insists you decide what to do about none. The tools for this are:

Tool Meaning Example
otherwise fallback value nickname otherwise "friend"
if … is x? branch on presence if find_user(id) is u?
match full control none -> … / u? -> …
? propagate none out of a function returning an optional user?
.expect(msg) assert presence; stops the program with msg otherwise config.expect("config required")
.or_error(msg) turn none into an error, usually followed by ? (§8.3) find_user(id).or_error("no such user")?

Plain dots through optionals

There is no ?. operator. A plain dot (a field, a method call, a chain of them) may look through an optional, but only where the chain is immediately consumed by something that deals with none:

The chain is consumed by… Example
(a) otherwise city = order.customer.address.city otherwise "unknown"
(b) postfix ? email = find_user(id).email? (returns none from the function)
(c) an is pattern or a match subject if order.customer.address is a?
(d) a position whose expected type is optional city: Text? = order.customer.address.city; return user.email in a function returning Text?; an argument to a Text? parameter

Anywhere else, a dot on a T? is a compile-time error that suggests the four ways out — a fallback with otherwise, propagation with ?, a branch with is, and, for an unannotated binding, annotating the optional type:

error: `order.customer` may be missing, so `.address` cannot be read here
  --> orders.vs:3:23
   |
 3 | city = order.customer.address.city
   |        ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ this is a `Customer?`
   |
help: say what happens when it is missing:
        city = order.customer.address.city otherwise "unknown"
        city = order.customer.address.city?           (return none)
        if order.customer is c?  …                     (branch)
      or keep it optional:   city: Text? = order.customer.address.city

The rules of a lifted chain:

  • It short-circuits completely. At the first none, the rest of the chain is not evaluated — later hops, method calls, and their arguments.
  • It yields one level of optional. A hop that itself returns X? does not create X??: "something along the chain was missing" is the only question a chain answers, so order.customer.nickname (with nickname: Text?) is a plain Text?. Lookups keep their own types: m.get(k) on a Map<Text, Int?> is still Int?? (below).
  • Ownership follows the view rule (§9.5): views flow along the chain and the end of the chain decides, exactly as for chains without optionals.
  • The optional's own methods win. .expect(msg), .or_error(msg) and .copy() on a V? act on the optional itself, not on the value inside: find_user(id).copy() is an owned User?. If a name is both a method of the optional and a field or method of the inner type, the call is a compile-time error that asks you to choose with is or otherwise.
