  • .or_error(msg) applies to the final result of the chain. In order.customer.address.city.or_error("no city")?, a none anywhere along the chain becomes the error.

Postfix ? is an ordinary postfix operator, applied left to right like a call or a field access (§3.8). A ? immediately followed by . is a compile-time error, because other languages read ?. as safe access: "?. is not Verse; write (a?).b to propagate then read, or a.b otherwise … / a.b? to look through the optional". The parenthesised (find_user(id)?).email is valid: it propagates a missing user out of the function and then reads .email from the User. find_user(id).email? reads through the optional and propagates if anything along the chain is missing. verse fmt never removes these parentheses.

Nested optionals are real

Style: avoid nested optionals such as T?? in public APIs; prefer a variant that names each case (type Reply = NoSuchKey | Pending | Value(v: Int)). The none? and score?? patterns below exist for generic code.

Outside lifted chains, optionals are never flattened: T?? is a different type from T?. This matters for lookups. map[key] and list.get(i) return V?, where V is the element type — so on a Map<Text, Int?> a lookup has type Int??, and "the key is missing" (none) stays distinguishable from "the key is present and its value is none" (a present none):

scores: Map<Text, Int?> = {"ana": 7, "bruno": none}

match scores["bruno"]          # Int??
    none -> print("no such player")
    none? -> print("bruno has not played yet")
    score?? -> print("score {score}")

On ordinary maps and lists (whose elements are not optional), lookups are plain V? and none of this comes up.

8.2 Fallible types T | E

A function that can fail declares it in its return type:

fn read_text(path: Text): Text | Error      # signatures only
fn parse_port(text: Text): Int | ParseError

ParseError is defined in std.num; it is the error type of Text.to_int(), which returns Int | ParseError (and of Text.to_float(), which returns Float | ParseError).

The body returns either a T (success) or an error value. A value of the error type returned as the last expression, or with return, is the failure:

fn divide(a: Float, b: Float): Float | Error
    if b == 0.0
        return error("division by zero")
    a / b

The Error trait

Error types implement the built-in Error trait:

trait Error: Show
    fn message(self): Text
    fn cause(self): Error?
        none

T | Error (with the trait name itself) accepts any error type — the most common choice for application code. Libraries often define specific error types:

type FetchError = NoResponse(seconds: Int) | BadStatus(code: Int) | Offline

impl Error for FetchError
    fn message(self): Text
        match self
            NoResponse(s) -> "no response after {s}s"
            BadStatus(c) -> "server answered {c}"
            Offline -> "no network connection"

The built-in function error(message: Text, cause: Error? = none): Error creates a simple error value.

8.3 Propagation with ?

Postfix ? means "stop early: if this is an error or missing, return it from the current function; otherwise give me the value."

import std.json
import read_text from std.fs

fn load_settings(path: Text): Settings | Error
    text = read_text(path)?
    data = json.parse(text)?
    Settings.from_json(data)

Rules for expr?:

expr has type enclosing function returns effect
T | E U | E on error, return that error; otherwise yields T
T | E U | Error on error, return it as Error; otherwise yields T
T | E U? compile-time error — an error cannot become none; handle it, or change the return type to U? | Error
T | E1 U | E2 (unrelated E2) compile-time error — convert with .context("…") (gives Error) or match
T? U? on none, return none; otherwise yields T
T? U | E compile-time error — say why with .or_error("…")
Error (widened) U | FetchError compile-time error — ? never narrows Error back to a specific type (§4.6)

Layers are peeled from the outside, in written order. For a type with several layers, ? and otherwise act on the outermost layer only. In Text? | Error, the outermost layer is the error side:

fn nickname(id: Int): Text? | Error
    ...

a = nickname(7)?                             # Text?  (errors propagated)
b = nickname(7) otherwise none               # Text?  (errors replaced by none)
c = nickname(7) otherwise "anonymous"        # error: right side must be `Text?`
d = nickname(7)? otherwise "anonymous"       # Text   (error propagated, then none handled)
e = nickname(7) otherwise none otherwise "anonymous"       # Text

The same rule makes an Int?? need two steps. In expressions, two postfix ? in a row are not allowed — write (x?)? — or use x otherwise none otherwise 0. (x?? exists only as a pattern, meaning "present and present", §7.5.)

Views and otherwise. a otherwise b is a view when both sides are views (text and number literals and other static data count as views), and owned when the right side is an owned temporary; in that case a view on the left needs .copy(), and leaving it out is a compile-time error that suggests it (§3.8.2):

greeting = args.first() otherwise "world"                  # a view
label = labels["x"].copy() otherwise build_label()         # owned
wrong = labels["x"] otherwise build_label()                # error: the left side
                                                           #   is a view; write
                                                           #   labels["x"].copy()

The full table, including an owned left side with a non-static view on the right (copy the right side), literals materialised in owned positions, and lifted chains on owned temporaries, is in §3.8.2.

Where ? returns to. ? always returns from the innermost function-like body that contains it:

? appears in… it returns from…
a named function that function
a lambda the lambda (its return type becomes fallible or optional; §5.4)
a function run with spawn the spawned function; the error is delivered by .wait() (§11.1)
a test block the test, which then fails with the error's message (§14.1)
entry-file top-level code the script, which exits (see below)

To turn a missing value into an error explicitly:

user = find_user(id).or_error("no user with id {id}")?

At the top level of a script (outside any function), ? on a failed value prints the error message to standard error and exits with status 1. On none it prints error: missing value at file.vs:LINE and exits with status 1.

8.4 Handling errors

import std.fs
import read_text from std.fs

# Fallback value
notes = read_text("notes.txt") otherwise ""

# Branch on success or failure
match read_text("notes.txt")
    text: Text -> print(text)
    err: Error -> print("could not read notes: {err.message()}")

# Add context while propagating
config_text = read_text(path).context("loading {path}")?

# Ignore a result on purpose (the only way; see below)
_ = fs.remove("cache.tmp")

.context(msg) wraps the error in a new error whose cause() is the original.

Fallible results cannot be dropped

Discarding a fallible value is a compile-time error. A call whose result is T | E cannot stand alone as a statement, and neither can a value that contains fallible results — a List<T | Error> from wait_all, a Map<K, V | E>, a tuple with a fallible part. Either handle it (?, otherwise, match, a loop over the results) or discard it visibly with _ = …:

fs.remove("cache.tmp")                 # error: result `Nothing | Error` is ignored
                                       #   help: add `?`, handle it, or write `_ = …`
fs.remove("cache.tmp")?                # propagate
_ = fs.remove("cache.tmp")             # deliberately ignored

8.5 Panics

Some failures are bugs, not conditions to handle: indexing a list out of range, integer overflow, dividing an integer by zero, a failed assert, or .expect(...) on none. These panic: the current task stops (running its with cleanups), the message and a stack trace are always printed to standard error at the moment of the panic, and — if the task is the main program — the program exits with status 101. A panic in a spawned task is delivered to its waiter as a TaskPanicked error (§11.2). Panics are not caught by ? and are not meant for normal control flow. Code that wants to avoid them uses the checked alternatives (items.get(i), a.checked_div(b)).

9. Collections

9.1 Lists

List<T> is an ordered, growable sequence.

nums = [1, 2, 3]
print(nums[0])                    # 1      — Int; out of range panics
print(nums.get(10))               # none   — Int?
print(nums.get(10, default: 0))   # 0      — Int
print(nums.len())                 # 3
print(nums[1..])                  # [2, 3]
print(nums[..2])                  # [1, 2]
print(nums + [4, 5])              # [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

mut queue: List<Text> = []
queue.push("first")
queue.push("second")
next = queue.pop_front()       # Text?
queue[0] = "changed"

Negative indices are not allowed; use nums.last() (which returns T?).

9.2 Maps

Map<K, V> associates keys with values. Insertion order is preserved when iterating: replacing the value of an existing key keeps its place, and a key that is removed and inserted again moves to the end.

ages = {"ana": 30, "bruno": 17}
print(ages["ana"])                    # 30 — Int? (present)
print(ages["zoe"])                    # none
print(ages.get("zoe", default: 0))    # 0  — Int

mut stock: Map<Text, Int> = {:}
stock["apples"] = 10                              # insert or replace
stock["apples"] = stock.get("apples", default: 0) + 5
_ = stock.remove("pears")                         # remove returns the old value, Int?
print("apples" in stock)                          # true

Writing map[key] = value inserts or replaces. Keys must implement Hash and Eq. Iterating a map — or calling map.entries() — yields labeled pairs (key: K, value: V), which can be destructured (for (name, age) in ages), passed to a two-parameter lambda (§5.4), or read by label (entry.key, entry.value). An empty map is written {:}; a bare {} is a compile-time error that points to {:} and set{}.

9.3 Lookups side by side

Lists and maps answer "what is at this position/key?" differently, on purpose:

Expression On a List<T> On a Map<K, V>
c[i] / m[k] T — panics if out of range V? — none if the key is missing
c.get(i) / m.get(k) T? V? (same as m[k])
c.get(i, default: x) / m.get(k, default: x) T — x if out of range V — x if missing
c[i] = v / m[k] = v replace (panics if out of range) insert or replace

A bad list index is almost always a bug (and loops over 0..items.len() should not need unwrapping), while a missing map key is ordinary data — see §18.11.

The one-argument get returns V? without flattening: on a Map<Text, Int?> it returns Int?? (§8.1). The two-argument get(key, default: x) always returns a plain V, never an optional, and is the idiomatic way to count or accumulate:

counts[word] = counts.get(word, default: 0) + 1

default: is a parameter of get only; it is not a general language feature. get(k, default: x) follows the same ownership table as otherwise (§3.8.2), with the element as the left side and the default as the right:

Element Default Result
a view (always, from a borrowed collection) a view or a static literal (0, "") a view: names.get(id, default: "anonymous")
a view an owned temporary (Text.new(), make_label()) owned, so the element side needs .copy(): write names.get(id, default: Text.new()) as names.get(id).copy() otherwise Text.new()

Without the copy, the second row is a compile-time error: a view of an owned temporary default would not outlive the call. names.get(id).copy() otherwise Text.new() is the intended way to get an owned element with an owned default. It works because .copy() on an optional view V? of a Copyable V yields an owned V? (none stays none), which then meets the owned default as in the second row of the otherwise table (.copy() is one of the optional's own methods, §8.1). Where an owned value is needed — storing it, returning it, sending it to a task — copy the view result: names.get(id, default: "anonymous").copy().

Ownership of lookups. list[i], m[k] and get give a view of the element — a second-class borrow that can be read, passed to functions, or bound to a name, but not stored in a field or collection, returned, or sent to a task. To keep an element beyond that, copy it (m["ana"].copy()) or take it out of a mut collection with remove/pop, which return owned values. Copy types (numbers, Bool, Char, and records made only of them) are simply copied.

Slices are views too. nums[1..], nums[2..5] and name[0..=2] give a view of part of the list or text, with the same rules as list[i]. Write nums[1..].copy() or name[0..=2].copy() to get an owned list or text.

9.4 Sets

Set<T> is a collection of unique values. It iterates in insertion order, exactly like Map (§9.2): adding a value that is already present keeps its place, and a value that is removed and added again moves to the end.

vowels = set{'a', 'e', 'i', 'o', 'u'}
seen: Set<Text> = set{}
print('e' in vowels)                 # true
both = set{"a", "b"}.union(set{"b", "c"})       # set{"a", "b", "c"}

Set operations: union, intersection, difference, is_subset, plus + (union) and - (difference) as conveniences. Their results keep the order of the left set; union then adds the right set's new values in its order.

9.5 Transforming collections

Collections share a rich family of methods (from the Iterable trait) that chain with dots and take lambdas. Chains read top to bottom like a recipe. A chain that is bound to a name or returned is evaluated eagerly and collected into a List at the end of the statement; only a chain used as a for target or consumed in the middle of a longer chain stays lazy, so a lazy iterator value is never stored, bound or returned. A collected chain that ends in an owning step is an owned List<…>; one that ends in adapters only is a local view (see Ownership below):

total = numbers.filter(n -> n % 2 == 0).map(n -> n * 2).sum()

top_scorers = players
    .filter(p -> p.active)
    .sort_by(.score, descending: true)
    .prefix(3)
    .map(.name.copy())
Method Result
map(f) apply f to each element
filter(pred) keep elements where pred is true
reduce(initial, f) combine into one value
sum(), product(), average() numeric summaries
min(), max(), min_by(key), max_by(key) the smallest or largest element, T? (a view)
count(), count(pred) number of elements (matching)
any(pred), all(pred) Bool
find(pred) first match, T? (a view)
first(), last() T? (a view)
sort(), sort_by(key, descending: false) a sorted list
group_by(key) Map<K, List<T>>
prefix(n), skip(n), prefix_while(p), skip_while(p) prefixes and suffixes
enumerate() (index, item) pairs
zip(other) pairs from two collections
flat_map(f), flatten() flatten nested collections (an owning step)
unique() remove duplicates, keeping first occurrences
reverse() the elements in reverse order
chunks(n), windows(n) groups of elements, each a view of a slice (§9.3)
join(sep) Text from a collection of Show values
to_list(), to_set(), to_map() collect into a concrete collection (an owning step)

Ownership: views flow through a chain; the end of the chain decides. These methods borrow the collection they are called on and pass each element to the lambda as a borrow. Nothing is ever copied silently:

  • Adapters pass views. Within one expression chain, the methods that hand elements along (filter, sort, sort_by, prefix, skip, prefix_while, skip_while, unique, reverse, zip, enumerate, …) pass second-class views of the source's elements. Nothing is copied.
  • The chain ends in an owning step, which decides what the result owns:
  • map(f) — the result holds what the lambda returns, which must be owned: .map(p -> p.age) copies an Int (a Copy type), while .map(p -> p.name) is an error that asks for .map(p -> p.name.copy()) (or the key path .map(.name.copy()));
  • a reduction (sum, count, join, any, all, reduce, …), which produces a new value;
  • a move out of an owned source at its last use (a temporary, or a binding that is not used afterwards), which moves the elements instead of copying them;
  • an explicit .copy(), which duplicates the remaining elements: people.filter(p -> p.active).copy() is an owned List<Person>;
  • a collecting step — to_list(), to_set(), to_map(), flat_map(f), flatten() — which builds a new owned collection: it moves the elements from a source at its last use, and otherwise needs .copy() before it. A bound or returned chain is collected into an owned list at the end of the statement, and side effects in its lambdas run then: tasks = urls.map(url -> spawn fetch(url.copy())) is a List<Task<…>> whose tasks are spawned when that statement executes. to_list() is needed only where the chain would otherwise be consumed as something else — as a for target, or to name the element type — not for binding. (chunks(n) and windows(n) are not owning steps: each group is a view of a slice of the source, §9.3.)
  • No implicit duplication of non-Copy elements. If a chain would have to duplicate an element that is not Copy to produce an owned result — for example adults: List<Person> = people.filter(p -> p.age >= 18) while people is still used later — that is a compile error with the usual suggestion: add .copy() (which needs Copyable, §10.4) or move the later use. Copy elements (numbers, Bool, Char, …) are copied implicitly as everywhere else.
  • Single-element results are views. find, first, last, min, max, min_by and max_by return a view of the element, as list[i], m[k] and get(k, default: x) do (§9.3). So people.find(p -> p.id == id).email otherwise "none" copies nothing, and keeping the element is written people.find(p -> p.id == id).copy() (an owned Person?; .copy() acts on the optional, §8.1). That is the rule for a borrowed source. On an owned source at its last use — a take parameter or a temporary — the single element moves out and the rest of the collection is freed; this is the owned counterpart of the view rule (see largest in §20.3).
  • A binding to a chain is a local view. adults = people.filter(…) is allowed when people is used later: adults is a view that lives only in the current scope, exactly like b = a (§4.9). It can be read, iterated and passed to functions, but not stored, returned or sent to a task.
adults = people.filter(p -> p.age >= 18)           # a local view; nothing copied
print(adults.len())
names = adults.map(.name.copy())                   # the one visible copy
oldest = people.max_by(.age).copy()                # an owned Person?
print(people.len())                                # `people` is still usable

Key functions. Comparison key functions (sort_by, min_by, max_by) may return views, so people.sort_by(.name) needs no copy of each name. group_by stores its keys in the resulting map, so its key function must return an owned value: people.group_by(.city.copy()). Its groups hold the elements themselves, so group_by is an owning step: it moves from a source at its last use, or needs .copy() before it.

min(), max() and average() on a possibly empty collection return T?; on a list known non-empty by the caller, combine with otherwise or .expect().

9.6 Equality and ordering

== and != compare structurally: two values are equal when they have the same type and equal contents. Because every value has a single owner and there are no references in the language, identity is never observable, so there is no separate identity comparison.

assert [1, 2] == [1, 2]
assert User(name: "A", age: 1) == User(name: "A", age: 1)
assert {"a": 1} == {"a": 1}

Built-in types, tuples, lists, records and variants whose parts are comparable automatically implement Eq; types whose parts are ordered automatically implement Order (lexicographic for tuples and lists; declaration order for variants; field order for records). Comparing values of different types is a compile-time error, with one convenience: a T may be compared with a T? (so counts["the"] == 3 works on a map lookup). Float equality follows IEEE 754 (nan != nan), so Float implements Eq only partially and cannot be a map key or set element; use std.num.OrderedFloat if needed.

10. Traits and generics

10.1 Traits

A trait names a set of methods that several types can share. A method without a body is required; a method with a body is a default that implementations may override. Because a required method has no body to infer from, its parameter and return types are always written in the trait; implementations may leave them out, since the trait already fixes them.

trait Speaker
    fn speak(self): Text

    fn speak_twice(self): Text
        "{self.speak()} {self.speak()}"

A type implements a trait with impl Trait for Type:

type Dog
    name: Text

type Robot
    model: Int

impl Speaker for Dog
    fn speak(self): Text
        "{self.name} says woof"

impl Speaker for Robot
    fn speak(self): Text
        "Unit {self.model} says beep"

A type's own methods go in a plain impl Type block; trait methods go in impl Trait for Type. An implementation must appear in the module that defines either the trait or the type (this keeps implementations easy to find and prevents conflicts between libraries).

10.2 Supertraits

A trait can require another trait:

trait Describe: Show
    fn describe(self): Text
        "<{self}>"

Every type implementing Describe must also implement Show.

10.3 Traits as types

A trait name used as a type means "any value whose type implements this trait". This allows collections of different types that share behavior:

speakers: List<Speaker> = [Dog(name: "Rex"), Robot(model: 7)]
for s in speakers
    print(s.speak())

Calls through a trait type are dispatched at run time.

10.4 Built-in traits

Trait Provides Automatically implemented?
Show show(self): Text, used by interpolation and print yes, structurally, for all types (override for custom text)
Eq ==, != yes, when all parts are Eq
Order <, <=, >, >=, sort() yes, when all parts are Order
Hash use as map key / set element yes, when all parts are Hash
Iterable<T> for … in, and all the methods of §9.5 lists, maps, sets, ranges, text, channel receivers
Default Type.default() when all fields have defaults
Cleanup cleanup(mut self), run automatically at the end of the owner's scope and by with (§13) no
Copy implicit copying on assignment and passing (§4.9); every Copy type is also Copyable yes, for scalars and for records, variants and tuples made only of Copy parts; cannot be implemented by hand
Copyable the .copy() method, with no arguments (a duplicate) or with field arguments on records (a duplicate with changes, §4.3) yes, structurally, for every type whose parts are all Copyable; absent for Task<T>, for types that implement Cleanup, and for anything that contains them by value (a record field, variant, tuple or collection element); cannot be implemented by hand in 0.1. The handles Shared<T>, Guarded<T>, Sender<T>, Weak<Shared<T>> and Weak<Guarded<T>> are always Copyable, whatever T is — including resources, as in Guarded<File> — because their .copy() copies the handle (a new reference to the same shared value) and never duplicates the value inside (§11.4); Receiver<T> is not Copyable in 0.1 (single consumer)
Index<K, V> x[k] reads (§9.3) lists, maps, text and slices; cannot be implemented by hand in 0.1
Error message(self), cause(self) no
Add, Sub, Mul, Div, Rem +, -, *, /, % Int, Float, std.num types; Add also for Text and List (concatenation)
Neg unary - Int, Float, std.num types

Copyable is deliberately closed in 0.1. It cannot be implemented by hand, and a type that implements Cleanup is deliberately not Copyable: duplicating a file handle, a lock guard or a temporary directory would run its cleanup twice or leave two owners of one external resource. A type that does need duplication offers an explicit method with its own name and its own meaning, such as duplicate() (for example, reopening the same file), so the call site says what really happens.

The arithmetic traits are how numeric types in std.num (such as Decimal and BigInt) and user types like vectors or money get operators. They are the only operator overloading Verse allows (§18.5); there is no way to define new operators or to overload and, or, not, otherwise, == (which comes from Eq) or indexing.

type Vector
    x: Float
    y: Float

impl Add for Vector
    fn add(self, other: Vector): Vector
        Vector(x: self.x + other.x, y: self.y + other.y)

v = Vector(x: 1.0, y: 2.0) + Vector(x: 0.5, y: 0.5)

10.5 Generic functions and types

Generic parameters go in angle brackets after the name.

fn first<T: Copyable>(items: List<T>): T?
    items.get(0).copy()           # `get` returns a view; the caller gets a copy

type Box<T>
    value: T

type Pair<A, B>
    left: A
    right: B

type Tree<T> = Leaf | Node(left: Tree<T>, value: T, right: Tree<T>)

Generic arguments are usually inferred: first([1, 2, 3]) is Int?, and Box(value: "hi") is a Box<Text>. Write them explicitly when needed: Box<Int>(value: 0), names: List<Text> = [].

Free generic functions do not take explicit type arguments in 0.1: their type arguments are inferred, or given by annotating the binding (n: Int = parse(text)?). parse<Int>(text) is a compile-time error whose help suggests that annotation. Explicit type arguments are allowed only on an associated function called through a type name, such as Channel.new<Int>(capacity: 10) (§11.4).

Methods on a generic type declare the parameters on the impl:

impl<T> Box<T>
    fn map<U>(self, f: fn(T): U): Box<U>
        Box(value: f(self.value))

10.6 Constraints

A generic parameter can require traits with :; several traits are joined with +.

fn largest<T: Order + Copyable>(items: List<T>): T?
    items.max().copy()            # `max` returns a view (§9.5); return a copy

fn announce<T: Speaker + Show>(who: T)
    print("{who}: {who.speak()}")

impl<T: Show> Show for Box<T>
    fn show(self): Text
        "Box({self.value})"

Generics are checked once, at definition: inside largest, only operations promised by Order and Copyable may be used on T. That includes the ownership check: a generic (or unannotated) parameter type is treated as an opaque, non-Copy type unless it has a Copy bound, so T values are never copied implicitly, and .copy() needs Copyable (§4.2, rule 9). Errors about a function's body appear at the definition. The only call-site errors are unmet bounds, written or inferred, and they name the bound. The compiler specializes generic code for speed; this is invisible to the programmer.

Copy and Copyable are different promises: T: Copy means a T is duplicated implicitly (numbers, all-scalar records); T: Copyable means a T can be duplicated explicitly with .copy() (almost everything, but not a Task or an open File).

11. Concurrency

11.1 Spawning tasks

spawn starts a function call running concurrently in a lightweight task and immediately returns a Task<T>, where T is the call's return type. .wait() blocks the current task until the result is ready.

Errors in a task surface at .wait(). Because anything can go wrong in another task — including a panic — .wait() always returns a fallible value, T | Error, which you handle like any other: with ?, otherwise, or match. If the spawned function is itself fallible, its errors arrive on the same error side. For a function returning Text | FetchError, .wait() would return Text | FetchError | Error, which normalizes to Text | Error (§4.6); use match with err: FetchError -> to recover the specific type. ? inside the spawned function returns from that function, and the error is what .wait() later reports.

import get from std.net

fn fetch(url)
    response = get("https://{url}")?
    response.body          # a field moved out of `response` at its last use (§4.9)

a = spawn fetch("a.com")
b = spawn fetch("b.com")

print(a.wait() otherwise "a failed")    # handle the failure here
page_b = b.wait()?                      # or stop early and pass it up
print(page_b)

There is no async/await and no function coloring. Any function can be spawned, and any function can call blocking operations like get or read_text: while one task waits for I/O, the runtime runs other tasks. Tasks are multiplexed over all CPU cores.

The arguments of a spawned call are evaluated before the task starts, in the spawning task. spawn applies to exactly one call expression; to spawn a small block of work, give it a name with fn and spawn the call.

Ownership across tasks

  • spawn f(x) moves x into the task. The task owns its arguments for the whole call, so a spawned function's parameters are always owned values, even when the function declares them as plain borrows.
  • A borrowed value cannot cross into a task. Inside a function, a borrowed parameter (or a view from list[i], a for loop over a still-used list, or a key-path) cannot be passed to spawn; pass .copy() instead. Tasks cannot borrow from the spawner in 0.1.
  • No mut arguments. spawn f(mut x) is a compile error: an exclusive borrow must end when the call returns, and a task cannot hand a mut borrow back to the spawner. Move the value in and get the changed value back from wait(), or share it through a Guarded<T>.
  • Using a value after spawning it is a use-after-move error. In a loop, the error is reported on the second iteration and suggests .copy():

verse config = load_config() for url in urls spawn crawl(url.copy(), config) # error: `config` moved into the task in # one iteration, used again in the next # help: spawn crawl(url.copy(), config.copy())

  • Handles are copied explicitly, and cheaply. Sender<T>, Shared<T>, Guarded<T> and Weak<Shared<T>> / Weak<Guarded<T>> values are handles. Passing one to spawn follows the same rule as every other value — it moves — so to keep using it, pass handle.copy(): a new handle to the same channel or shared value, not a copy of the value inside (§11.4). There is no implicit copy on spawn. A Receiver<T> is not Copyable: it is moved into the one task that consumes the channel.

11.2 Working with many tasks

import wait_all, wait_any from std.task

tasks = urls.map(url -> spawn fetch(url.copy()))       # `url` is a borrow: copy it
pages = wait_all(tasks)                  # takes the tasks; List<Text | Error>, in order

mirrors = mirror_urls.map(url -> spawn fetch(url.copy()))
fastest = wait_any(mirrors)?             # the first to finish; the others are cancelled
Operation Signature Meaning
task.wait() wait(take self): T | Error block until done; consumes the task
task.wait(timeout: d) wait(take self, timeout: Duration): T | Error the same, failing with a Timeout error if it takes too long
task.is_done() is_done(self): Bool never blocks
task.cancel() cancel(self) request cancellation (§11.5)
wait_all(tasks) wait_all<T>(take tasks: List<Task<T>>): List<T | Error> results in task order
wait_any(tasks) wait_any<T>(take tasks: List<Task<T>>): T | Error the first result to complete; the rest are cancelled

Remember that List<T | Error> contains fallible results, so the value of wait_all cannot be discarded (§8.4) — loop over it, or _ = it on purpose.

Panics in tasks. If a task panics, the panic message and stack trace are printed to standard error immediately, at the moment of the panic — whether or not anyone handles it later. The waiter then receives a value of the named error type TaskPanicked (from std.task, implementing Error, with message() and trace()), which match can tell apart from ordinary errors:

import TaskPanicked from std.task

match task.wait()
    page: Text -> show(page)
    crash: TaskPanicked -> alert_on_call(crash.message())
    err: Error -> print("fetch failed: {err.message()}")

The task boundary is the one place where a panic becomes a value, so one failing request cannot bring down a whole server — but because the panic was already printed, task.wait() otherwise "failed" can never hide a bug.

11.3 Structured lifetimes

Tasks belong to the function (or script) that spawned them. When that function finishes, any of its tasks that were never waited on are waited for automatically before it returns. If such an unwaited task failed (with an error, a panic, or cancellation), its error is reported on standard error and the process will exit with a non-zero status (1, or 101 for a panic) when it finishes, even if everything else succeeded. This status applies only when the program ends naturally: an explicit exit(code) always wins, and its code is the one the process returns. Discarding a Task value (a bare spawn worker(…) statement) is therefore allowed — an accepted exception to the rule that fallible results cannot be dropped, because its outcome cannot be lost. A task therefore never outlives the code that started it, results are never silently lost, and a program ends only after all of its work is done. To deliberately run something in the background beyond the current function, return its Task or pass it to someone who will wait on it.

11.4 Sharing data safely

A task owns what it was given (§11.1), so two tasks can never touch the same value by accident, and data races are impossible. Sharing is opt-in and always goes through one of these handle types from std.task:

Handle Meaning Copying the handle
Sender<T> the sending end of a channel: send owned values to the task that holds the Receiver a new sender to the same channel
Receiver<T> the receiving end of a channel; single consumer in 0.1 not copyable; it moves (fan-out uses several channels)
Shared<T> shared read-only ownership: the value is freed when the last handle goes away (atomically reference-counted) shares the value; nobody can change it
Guarded<T> shared mutable state behind a lock: read it inside with g.lock() as value, change it inside with g.lock() as mut value shares the value
Weak<Shared<T>>, Weak<Guarded<T>> a non-owning handle, parameterised over the handle it was made from: h.downgrade() on a Shared<T> gives a Weak<Shared<T>>, and on a Guarded<T> a Weak<Guarded<T>>; upgrade() returns Shared<T>? or Guarded<T>? respectively (none if the value is gone) a new weak handle to the same value; keeps nothing alive
Task<T> the result of spawn (§11.1) not copyable; wait takes it

Sender, Shared, Guarded and Weak are Copyable (§10.4) whatever their inner type — even Guarded<File> — and their .copy() copies the handle: it returns a new reference to the same shared value and never duplicates the value inside. As everywhere else, the copy is written explicitly — including when a handle is passed to spawn. Receiver<T> is not Copyable in 0.1. Weak accepts only a Shared or Guarded handle; Sender and Receiver are not weakable, so Weak<Sender<T>> and Weak<Receiver<T>> are compile errors (a channel closes when its last Sender is dropped, never by weak reference).

These are the only types whose copies refer to the same value; everything else in Verse has exactly one owner. They are also the only way to build a cycle (§4.10): a cycle of Shared/Guarded handles is never freed, so back-pointers should be Weak.

Channels send values from one task to another. Channel.new<T>() returns a pair (tx, rx): a Sender<T> and a Receiver<T>. send takes its value, so ownership moves to the task that receives it. Senders are copied (one per producing task); the receiver is moved to the single consuming task. The channel closes when its last Sender is dropped. The capacity defaults to 16; capacity: 0 makes an unbuffered (rendezvous) channel, where each send waits for a matching recv. The type argument is usually inferred from an annotation instead of written: (tx, rx): (Sender<Int>, Receiver<Int>) = Channel.new(capacity: 10).

import Channel, wait_all from std.task

fn worker(id, out)
    out.send(id * id)?                   # `Closed` if the receiver is gone

fn start_workers(take tx, count)         # spawns and returns, without waiting
    (1..=count).map(id -> spawn worker(id, tx.copy()))   # a Sender per task

(tx, rx) = Channel.new<Int>(capacity: 4)
tasks = start_workers(tx, 20)            # `tx` moves; 20 values, room for 4
for square in rx                         # consume while the producers run;
    print(square)                        #   ends when every Sender is gone
for outcome in wait_all(tasks)
    outcome?                             # stop if any worker failed

Waiting for the producers before consuming can deadlock once the channel is full, so always consume while the producers run, and wait for them afterwards. send is fallible: discarding its result is the usual compile-time error for an unhandled fallible value (§8.4). Closed is a named error type in std.task, like Timeout.

A Receiver given to another task moves, like any non-copyable value: spawn consume(rx).

Operation Signature Meaning
Channel.new<T>(…) new<T>(capacity: Int = 16): (Sender<T>, Receiver<T>) a new channel and its two ends; capacity: 0 is unbuffered (rendezvous)
tx.send(v) send(self, take value: T): Nothing | Closed blocks while the channel is full; returns the error Closed if the Receiver was dropped or the channel was closed — including for a sender already blocked on a full channel, which wakes with Closed
tx.close() close(self) an early shortcut: closes the channel for everyone, even while other Senders exist; the receiver drains what is left
rx.recv() recv(self): T? blocks until a value arrives; none once the channel is closed and drained

for value in rx receives until the channel is closed and drained (that is, until recv() returns none).

Shared read-only data — a large configuration, a dictionary, a parsed model — is wrapped once in Shared<T> and handed to as many tasks as needed without copying the data:

import Shared from std.task

dictionary = Shared(load_words("words.txt"))

fn check(text, words)
    text.words().filter(w -> not words.get().contains(w)).len()

a = spawn check(chapter_one, dictionary.copy())       # a new handle, same words
b = spawn check(chapter_two, dictionary)              # last use: the handle moves

shared.get() gives a read-only view of the value inside.

Shared mutable state is wrapped in Guarded<T> and can only be touched inside a with block that holds its lock:

import Guarded, wait_all from std.task

hits = Guarded(0)

fn record(counter)
    with counter.lock() as mut value
        value += 1

tasks = (1..=100).map(_ -> spawn record(hits.copy()))       # one handle per task
for outcome in wait_all(tasks)
    outcome?                       # stop if any task failed
with hits.lock() as value
    print("hits: {value}")

Inside with guarded.lock() as value, value is an exclusive borrow of the protected value; it is mutable only when written as mut value, as with every other binding (§3.9), so with g.lock() as value followed by value += 1 is the usual immutable-name error. The lock is released when the block ends, even if it ends early. Like every borrow, value cannot escape the block.

This is the one place where with … as binds something other than the resource itself. lock() returns a lock guard, and the guard type implements Cleanup (its cleanup releases the lock), so with cleans it up like any resource. But with on a guard binds the value inside the guard, as an exclusive borrow (mutable with as mut value), rather than the guard. No other type has this behaviour (§13.1).

11.5 Cancellation and time

task.cancel() asks a task to stop. Cancellation is cooperative: the task is stopped at its next blocking point — I/O, wait, sleep, send, or recv.

Cancellation cannot be caught inside the cancelled task. At the blocking point, the task unwinds exactly as it would for a panic: it stops running ordinary code, its with blocks close their resources in reverse order, and nothing — not otherwise, not match, not ? — can intercept it. So get(url) otherwise "x" cannot swallow a cancellation and keep going. Unlike a panic, a cancellation prints nothing. The waiter sees the outcome as a Cancelled error (from std.task) returned by .wait(), which it may handle normally.

Because cancellation never appears as a value inside the task, blocking operations keep simple signatures:

Operation Signature
std.time.sleep(d) sleep(duration: Duration) — returns Nothing; pauses only the current task
rx.recv() recv(self): T?
task.wait() wait(take self): T | Error (a cancelled child shows up here as Cancelled)

12. Modules

12.1 Files are modules

Every .vs file is a module named after its path relative to the project's src/ directory (or the directory of the entry file for single-file scripts):

my_app/
├── verse.toml
└── src/
    ├── main.vs            # module main
    ├── shapes.vs          # module shapes
    └── geometry/
        └── vectors.vs     # module geometry.vectors

12.2 Importing

import std.fs                       # use as fs.read_text(...)
import std.json as js               # use as js.parse(...)
import geometry.vectors             # use as vectors.add(...)
import get, post from std.net       # use get(...) and post(...) directly
import Shape, area from shapes
import parse as parse_json, stringify from std.json   # rename one item

import a.b.c binds the last segment (c) as a name; import a.b.c as d binds it as d. import x, y from M binds individual items, and import x as y from M binds the item x under the name y (useful when two modules export the same name); as can follow any name in the list, as in import parse as parse_json, stringify from std.json. The line always starts with import, so every import reads the same way: what you get first, where it comes from last. Whether a line imports a module or items is decided by the trailing from M on the same logical line: import a as b imports the module a as b, while import a as b from m imports the item a of m as b; without from, the names are module paths. An import must therefore fit on one line, or put a long item list in parentheses, which may span lines:

import (
    open, read_text, write_text,
    create as create_file,
) from std.fs

A renamed item keeps its kind: a type must be renamed to an uppercase-first name, a value to a lowercase one (§3.5). Wildcard imports do not exist; every name in a file can be traced to a declaration or an import. Imports must appear at the top of a file, after the module doc comment. Circular imports between modules are allowed for declarations but not for module-level constant initialization.

An imported name may be hidden by a local, and an import may hide a prelude name (with a warning); the rules are in §3.9.

Unused imports. An imported name that the file never uses is a warning on the import line. Unlike an unused binding (§3.9), it cannot be silenced, not even with a leading _: the fix is to delete the name, or the whole line. An import never adds code by itself; it only makes names visible (§12.4), and a build includes only what the program actually uses.

12.3 Visibility with export

Everything is private to its module by default. Mark items public with export:

## Geometry helpers.

export type Vector
    export x: Float
    export y: Float

export type Account
    export owner: Text
    cents: Int = 0                  # hidden: only this module can see it

impl Account
    export fn balance(self): Int
        self.cents

export fn add(a: Vector, b: Vector): Vector
    Vector(x: a.x + b.x, y: a.y + b.y)

export origin = Vector(x: 0.0, y: 0.0)

fn helper(): Int          # not exported: visible only in this module
    42

One word, one default, everywhere. export can precede fn, type, alias, trait, a module-level constant, record fields, and functions inside an impl. Anything not marked export — including a field of an exported record — is visible only inside its own module. Other modules can construct a record directly only if every field without a default is exported; otherwise they use an exported function such as Account.open(owner:). Trait implementations are public whenever both the trait and the type are visible.

Fields and methods share one namespace per type: a type cannot have a field and a method with the same name, whether or not either is exported (balance the field and balance() the method would be a compile error, which is why the field above is named cents).

Exported signatures and verse.api

Exported functions may leave their types to inference, just like private ones — there is no rule that exported functions must annotate their parameters. This is safe because of three guarantees:

  1. (a) A generated interface file is committed. verse api update writes verse.api at the package root, recording every exported item with its full inferred signature (including inferred constraints and parameter modes). The file is committed with the code.
  2. (b) The public API cannot drift silently. Every build re-infers the exported signatures and compares them with verse.api. If one differs, the build fails and shows the old and new signature, until someone runs verse api update on purpose (and the change shows up in review as a diff of verse.api). Editing a function body can therefore never change the public API by accident.
  3. (c) Inference never crosses a module boundary. Other modules — and other packages — are type-checked against verse.api (and the interface records of the package's own modules), never against another module's body.
## Geometry helpers.

export fn scale(v, factor)        # recorded in verse.api as:
    v.copy(x: v.x * factor, y: v.y * factor)

# verse.api (generated by `verse api update`; do not edit)
module geometry
fn scale<V, F>(v: V, factor: F): V
    where V has copy(x:, y:), V has field x: F, V has field y: F, F: Mul

The interface file uses a documented notation for inferred structural constraints (has field, has method) that cannot be written in source in 0.1 (§4.2). Annotating an exported function narrows what verse.api records, which is often what a library author wants.

12.4 Module contents

Only the entry file — the file passed to verse run — runs top-level statements. Imported modules may contain only declarations (fn, type, alias, trait, impl, test, import) and module-level constants (name = expr). Importing a module therefore never has side effects.

A top-level binding name = expr behaves in the only way that makes sense in each place:

  • In an imported module, a top-level binding is a constant. It is initialized once, on first use, and its initializer must be infallible: ? is not allowed, and its type may not be fallible, because a lazy initializer has no caller to return an error to. (mut is not allowed at module level.)

verse export max_retries = 3 # fine export default_port = 8080 # fine config = read_text("config.toml")? # error: module constants cannot fail

  • In the entry file, a top-level binding is an ordinary statement: it runs in order, top to bottom, like every other statement there, and may use ? (see §8.3 for what a failed top-level ? does). Such a binding is a script local: it is visible to the top-level statements after it, but not inside fn bodies (nor in impl methods or test blocks). A function that needs the value takes it as an argument. This keeps every function meaningful on its own — it never depends on whether a binding below it has run yet — and matches §14.1, where tests never run top-level statements. Module constants in imported modules are the only module-wide values.

```verse config = load_config("app.toml")?

fn port(config) # takes it as an argument config.port

print(port(config)) ```

Entry-file locals are not visible in functions (M-2), so the parameter config is not shadowing.

12.5 Program entry

A Verse program is a script: the entry file's top-level statements run from top to bottom.

print("Hello, {args.first() otherwise "world"}!")
  • args is a built-in List<Text> of command-line arguments, not including the program name (verse run hello.vs Ana gives args == ["Ana"]).
  • Top-level statements are the only entry mechanism. Verse 0.1 has no fn main; a function named main is just an ordinary function that runs only if the script calls it.
  • Exit status: 0 on normal completion; 1 if a top-level ? fails (the error message is printed to standard error) or if an unwaited task failed (§11.3); 101 on a panic; or any value passed to exit(code). An explicit exit(code) always overrides the failed-unwaited-task status, which applies only when the program ends naturally.

13. Resource management

13.1 with blocks

External resources — files, network connections, locks, temporary directories — must be released promptly and reliably. Because every value has one owner and is freed at the end of its owner's scope (§4.10), a type that implements the Cleanup trait is cleaned up automatically when its owner's scope ends, however it ends: normally, by return, break, continue, ? propagation, or a panic.

trait Cleanup
    fn cleanup(mut self)       # must not fail

That automatic cleanup is a safety net: a file you open in a function is closed when the function ends, even if you forget about it. The with statement is the explicit way to say exactly where a resource's life ends. It acquires the resource, binds it to a name for the indented block, and cleans it up when the block ends:

import open from std.fs

with open("log.txt")? as file
    for line in file.lines()
        print(line)
# file is closed here, not at the end of the function

with … as name binds the resource itself, with one documented exception: a lock guard. with guarded.lock() as value (§11.4) cleans up the guard (releasing the lock) like any other resource, but binds value to the protected value inside the guard, as an exclusive borrow (mutable only with as mut value). Lock guards are the only type that behaves this way.

The same mut rule applies to every resource: File's write methods (write_line, write, flush) take mut self, so a file you write to is bound with as mut: with create("out.txt")? as mut target.

cleanup must not fail: it has nowhere to report an error, because it may run during a panic or while another error is propagating. Types whose closing can fail (a buffered writer that must flush) also offer an explicit, fallible method — file.finish()? — to call when the error matters; cleanup is the quiet fallback.

13.2 Acquisition failure

Acquiring a resource can fail: open returns File | Error. with never propagates anything by itself. Its resource expression must be a value whose type implements Cleanup, so a fallible acquisition needs an explicit ?, exactly as anywhere else:

import open from std.fs

with open("log.txt")? as file          # `?` propagates a failed open
    ...

with open("log.txt") as file           # error: `File | Error` does not implement Cleanup
    ...                                #   help: add `?` to propagate the error

So with means one thing — clean this up when the block ends — and every early exit is still marked by ? or return. Infallible acquisitions such as counter.lock() (§11.4) need no ?.

To handle the failure locally, acquire first and decide:

match open("log.txt")                  # File | Error
    err: Error -> print("no log yet: {err.message()}")
    file: File ->
        with file as log               # `file` moves into the `with`
            print(log.read_all())

13.3 Several resources

Several resources can be acquired in one with, separated by commas. They are cleaned up in reverse order of acquisition.

import open, create from std.fs

with open("input.txt")? as source, create("output.txt")? as mut target
    for line in source.lines()
        target.write_line(line.upper())?

13.4 Custom resources

import std.fs
import std.random

type TempDir
    path: Text

impl TempDir
    fn create()                            # inferred: TempDir | Error
        path = "/tmp/verse-{random.int(0..1_000_000)}"
        fs.make_dir(path)?
        TempDir(path:)

impl Cleanup for TempDir
    fn cleanup(mut self)
        _ = fs.remove_all(self.path)       # ignore failures during cleanup

with TempDir.create()? as dir
    fs.write_text("{dir.path}/scratch.txt", "draft")?
    ...

_ = … discards a result deliberately; cleanup must not fail, because it may run during a panic.

14. Testing and docs

14.1 Test blocks

Tests are written next to the code they test, using test blocks:

fn slugify(title: Text): Text
    title.lower().words().join("-")

test "slugify joins lowercase words with dashes"
    assert slugify("Hello Big World") == "hello-big-world"

test "slugify of empty text is empty"
    assert slugify("") == ""
  • A test block has a descriptive text name and an indented body.
  • test blocks are ignored by verse run and verse build, and compiled only by verse test.
  • verse test never runs the entry file's top-level statements. Tests see the module's declarations (functions, types, traits, impls) and its module-level constants only. So testing a script such as §20.1 does not read files, and testing §20.2 does not touch the network or call exit. Code that a test needs must therefore live in a function, not in top-level statements.
  • A test passes if its body finishes without a failed assert, a panic, or a failed ?. Inside a test, ? returns from the test (which then fails with the error's message): test bodies behave like functions returning Nothing | Error.
  • Tests can access private items of their module.
  • Tests run in parallel, each in its own task; they must not depend on each other's order.

14.2 assert

assert condition checks a Bool. On failure it reports the source text and, for comparisons, the values of both sides:

FAIL  slugify joins lowercase words with dashes   (text.vs:4)
    assert slugify("Hello Big World") == "hello-big-world"
    left:  "hello-big--world"
    right: "hello-big-world"

An optional message follows a comma: assert total > 0, "cart cannot be empty". Outside tests, assert is also allowed in ordinary code, where a failure panics. Assertions are never removed from release builds.

Patterns combine with is for expressive checks:

test "parsing rejects letters"
    assert parse_age("abc") is _: Error
    assert parse_age("42")? == 42

14.3 Doc comments

## comments are Markdown. Where a ## block belongs is decided by one visible rule:

  • A ## block directly above a declaration, with no blank line in between, documents that declaration.
  • A ## block at the top of a file followed by a blank line documents the module.

verse fmt enforces the blank line after a module doc, so the two never look alike:

## Geometry helpers for 2-D drawings.     ← module doc (blank line follows)

import std.math

## The distance between two points.       ← documents `distance`
export fn distance(a: Point, b: Point): Float
    ...

Code blocks inside doc comments are doc tests: verse test runs them too.

## Returns the area of a shape.
##
## ```verse
## assert area(Square(side: 2.0)) == 4.0
## ```
export fn area(shape: Shape): Float
    ...

verse doc turns doc comments into a browsable HTML site, with every type, function, trait and implementation cross-linked.

15. Standard library overview

The standard library is small, consistent, and readable. Every module follows the same conventions: functions that can fail return T | Error (or a module-specific error type); functions that may find nothing return T?; resources implement Cleanup.

15.1 The prelude

These names are available in every file without importing. A local or a file-level import may hide one (an import warns); see §3.9.

Name Description
print(value: Show = "", end: Text = "\n") write value to standard output followed by end; print() with no argument writes an empty line
input(prompt: ""): Text? read a line from standard input; none at end of input
args List<Text> of command-line arguments
env(name): Text? read an environment variable
exit(code: Int) end the program immediately with a status code
error(message, cause: none): Error build a simple error
Types Int, Float, Bool, Char, Text, Bytes, Nothing, List, Map, Set, Range, Task
Traits Show, Eq, Order, Hash, Iterable, Index, Default, Cleanup, Copy, Copyable, Error, Add, Sub, Mul, Div, Rem, Neg

Error is a trait, not a type. Written where a type is expected, as in T | Error, a trait name means "any type that implements it" (§8.2, §10.3), which is why Error appears in return types throughout this spec.

File access is not in the prelude: there is exactly one name for each idea, and it lives in std.fs — open(path): File | Error (read), create(path): File | Error (write), and read_text(path): Text | Error (whole file at once). Import them with import open, read_text from std.fs.

15.2 Core modules

Module Purpose Highlights
std.fs files and directories read_text, write_text, append_text, read_bytes, exists, list_dir, walk, make_dir, remove, remove_all, open, create, File
std.net networking and HTTP get, post, put, delete, Request, Response(status, headers, body), serve, TcpStream, Url
std.text text processing words, lines, pad, wrap, similarity, Regex, Builder, Unicode normalization
std.time dates, times and durations now(), today(), sleep(d), Duration (5.seconds(), 200.millis(), 2.hours()), Instant, Date, DateTime, time zones, format
std.json JSON parse(text): Json | Error, stringify(value, pretty: false), the Json variant type, ToJson / FromJson traits with automatic implementations for records and variants
std.task concurrency Channel (Channel.new<T>() returns a Sender<T> and a Receiver<T>), Shared, Guarded, Weak, wait_all, wait_any, and the named error types Timeout, Cancelled, TaskPanicked and Closed (returned by Sender.send once the channel is closed); .copy() on Sender, Shared, Guarded and Weak copies the handle, explicitly, also when passing it to spawn; Receiver is not copyable and moves (§11.4)
std.math mathematics pi, e, sqrt, sin, cos, log, clamp
std.num numeric types sized integers, BigInt, Decimal, OrderedFloat, parsing, and ParseError, the error returned by Text.to_int() (Int | ParseError) and Text.to_float() (Float | ParseError)
std.random randomness int(range), float(), choice(list), shuffle(list), seeded generators
std.process child processes run(cmd, args), Output(status, stdout, stderr)
std.env environment vars(), current_dir(), home_dir(), platform
std.cli argument parsing declarative flags from a record type
std.log structured logging info, warn, error, levels, sinks

Domain libraries (finance, ml, web, gui, iot) ship as optional packages, not in std (§16.3).

A few examples:

import std.fs
import std.json
import std.time
import get from std.net

started = time.now()

response = get("https://api.example.com/items")?
items = json.parse(response.body)?

fs.write_text("items.json", json.stringify(items, pretty: true))?

names = fs.list_dir(".")?
for name in names.filter(n -> n.ends_with(".vs"))
    print(name)

print("done in {time.now() - started}")

json values can be converted to and from records directly:

type Item
    id: Int
    title: Text

raw = r"""
    {"id": 1, "title": "Pen"}
    """                                   # raw: `{` is not interpolation
item = Item.from_json(json.parse(raw)?)?
print(json.stringify(item))

16. Tooling

Verse ships as a single command, verse, that contains the compiler, runner, formatter, test runner, documentation generator, language server and package manager.

Command Purpose
verse run file.vs [args…] compile (cached) and run a script or project
verse test [path] run test blocks and doc tests; --filter "name", --watch
verse fmt [path] format code in the one canonical style; --check for CI
verse check type-check without running; fast feedback for editors
verse build produce an optimized native executable
verse build --size-report build, and list every included item with its size and why it was included
verse why <item> show the chain of uses from the program's entry statements to one included item
verse run --deny <capability> run, refusing a system capability named after its std module (net, fs, process, …); a program that can reach it fails before it starts
verse check --target <T> check that everything the program can reach is available on target T (no std.fs on a browser WebAssembly target, for example)
verse doc generate HTML documentation from doc comments
verse repl interactive prompt
verse new name create a project skeleton
verse add pkg / verse remove pkg manage dependencies
verse update update dependencies within allowed versions
verse publish publish a package to the registry
verse lsp language server for editors, including inline hints for inferred types
verse api update regenerate verse.api, the committed interface file of exported signatures (§16.4)
verse api check compare inferred exported signatures with verse.api (run by every build)

16.1 The formatter

verse fmt has no configuration options. It normalizes indentation to four spaces, spacing around operators, blank lines between declarations and trailing commas in multi-line lists; wraps long method chains one call per line; sorts imports; enforces the blank line after a module doc (§14.3); and drops the redundant ) that the lambda closing rule makes unnecessary (§5.4). It never removes semantically significant parentheses — those that end a lifted chain, and those in (a?).b, where a?.b would be an error (§8.1). It never inserts or removes type annotations: whether to spell out a type is the author's choice, and inferred types are shown by the editor as inline hints instead. A file that passes verse fmt --check looks the same as every other Verse file in the world.

16.2 Compiler messages

Error messages are written in plain language, point at the exact code, and suggest a fix where possible:

error: `email` might be missing
  --> users.vs:12:11
   |
12 |     print(user.email.lower())
   |           ^^^^^^^^^^ this is `Text?`, not `Text`
   |
help: provide a fallback:   user.email.lower() otherwise ""
help: or stop early:        print(user.email.lower()?)
help: or branch:            if user.email is email?  …

16.3 Packages

A project is described by verse.toml:

[package]
name = "word-tools"
version = "0.3.0"
description = "Small text utilities"
license = "MIT"
verse = "0.1"

[dependencies]
colors = "1.2"              # semantic versioning: >= 1.2.0, < 2.0.0
http_extra = { git = "https://example.com/http_extra.git", tag = "v0.4.1" }

[dev-dependencies]
snapshot = "0.9"
  • Packages are fetched from the central registry (or git/path sources) and pinned in verse.lock, which is committed for applications.
  • A package's modules are imported by package name: import red, bold from colors.
  • Resolution chooses a single version of each package per major version.
  • Builds are reproducible: the same verse.lock gives the same build.
  • Packages declare no install scripts; building a dependency cannot run arbitrary code.
  • A published package includes its verse.api; dependents are checked against it, never against the package's source.

A library package may add a [library] section that describes what it offers:

[library]
modules      = ["colors", "colors.term"]   # the modules dependents may import
capabilities = ["stdio"]                   # the system capabilities its code may reach
size_budget  = "40K"                       # `verse publish` fails if its example build exceeds it

[library.targets]                          # where the package is available
default      = "all"
unavailable  = []                          # targets it does not support

[library.native]                           # reserved for 0.2, with `extern` (§18.15)
links        = []                          # native libraries to link: data, never scripts

Domain libraries are first-party optional packages, not part of std: finance, ml, web, gui and iot are added with verse add like any other package. std.net.serve remains in std.

16.4 Interface files (verse.api)

verse.api is what makes inferred exported signatures safe (§12.3):

Step What happens
verse api update infers every exported signature and writes verse.api; commit it
verse build, verse check, verse test re-infer exported signatures; fail if any differs from verse.api, printing the recorded and the new signature
other modules and packages are checked against verse.api only — inference never crosses a module boundary

So the only way to change a public signature is to change the code and run verse api update, which turns the change into a visible diff in review. verse fmt never touches verse.api and never inserts annotations into source.

17. EBNF grammar sketch

This grammar is a readable sketch of the core language, not a complete formal definition. The lexer turns leading whitespace into INDENT and DEDENT tokens and ends logical lines with NEWLINE, suppressing it inside brackets, after a trailing binary operator, and before a line that begins with . or | (§3.4). BLANK is an empty line, significant only after a module doc. Text in "quotes" is a literal token; { x } means zero or more, [ x ] means optional, | separates alternatives. Rules marked (semantic) are checked after parsing.

(* ---------- Files and declarations ---------- *)
file          = { NEWLINE } [ doc BLANK ] { import } { top_item } ;
                                    (* doc + blank line = module doc (§14.3) *)
top_item      = declaration | statement | test_block ;
declaration   = [ doc ] [ "export" ]
                ( fn_decl | type_decl | alias_decl | trait_decl | binding )
              | [ doc ] impl_block ;
doc           = DOC_COMMENT { DOC_COMMENT } ;     (* directly above its item *)

import        = "import" module_path [ "as" IDENT ] NEWLINE
              | "import" ( import_list | "(" import_list [ "," ] ")" )
                "from" module_path NEWLINE ;
                (* the line always starts with `import`; a trailing `from` on
                   the same logical line makes the names items of that module,
                   so `import a as b` is a module and `import a as b from m` an
                   item. An import is one line; only the parenthesised list may
                   span lines (§3.4). *)
import_list   = import_item { "," import_item } ;
import_item   = name [ "as" name ] ;              (* same kind on both sides *)
name          = IDENT | TYPE_IDENT ;
module_path   = IDENT { "." IDENT } ;

(* ---------- Functions ---------- *)
fn_decl       = "fn" IDENT [ generics ] "(" [ params ] ")" [ ":" type ] block ;
fn_sig        = "fn" IDENT [ generics ] "(" [ params ] ")" [ ":" type ] NEWLINE ;
params        = param { "," param } [ "," ] ;
param         = [ "mut" | "take" ] "self"
              | [ "mut" | "take" ] IDENT [ ":" type ] [ "=" expr ] ;
                (* types optional (§4.2); `mut`/`take` always explicit *)
generics      = "<" generic_param { "," generic_param } ">" ;
generic_param = TYPE_IDENT [ ":" bound { "+" bound } ] ;
bound         = TYPE_IDENT [ type_args ] ;

(* ---------- Types ---------- *)
type_decl     = "type" TYPE_IDENT [ generics ]
                ( NEWLINE INDENT field { field } DEDENT    (* record: nothing after the name *)
                | "=" variant { "|" variant } NEWLINE ) ;  (* new variants; never a field block *)
                (* (semantic) a variant name may not be a type already in scope:
                   `type Meters = Float` is rejected with "use alias" *)
field         = [ doc ] [ "export" ] IDENT ( ":" type [ "=" expr ] | "=" expr ) NEWLINE ;
                (* the annotation may be omitted only when a default implies the type *)
variant       = TYPE_IDENT [ "(" field_list ")" ] ;
field_list    = IDENT ":" type { "," IDENT ":" type } [ "," ] ;
alias_decl    = "alias" TYPE_IDENT [ generics ] "=" type NEWLINE ;  (* incl. unions *)

type          = union_type ;
union_type    = optional_type { "|" optional_type } ;   (* normalized, §4.6 *)
optional_type = base_type { "?" } ;                       (* T?? is not T? *)
base_type     = { IDENT "." } TYPE_IDENT [ type_args ]      (* `time.Duration` *)
              | "(" type "," type { "," type } ")"               (* tuple   *)
              | "(" labeled { "," labeled } ")"                   (* labeled *)
              | "fn" "(" [ type { "," type } ] ")" ":" type
              | "(" type ")" ;
labeled       = IDENT ":" type ;
type_args     = "<" type { "," type } ">" ;

(* ---------- Traits and impls ---------- *)
trait_decl    = "trait" TYPE_IDENT [ generics ] [ ":" bound { "+" bound } ]
                NEWLINE INDENT { [ doc ] ( fn_sig | fn_decl ) } DEDENT ;
impl_block    = "impl" [ generics ] [ bound "for" ] type
                NEWLINE INDENT { [ doc ] [ "export" ] fn_decl } DEDENT ;

(* ---------- Statements ---------- *)
block         = NEWLINE INDENT statement { statement } DEDENT ;
statement     = binding | assign_stmt | if_stmt | loop_stmt
              | with_stmt | match_expr | exit_stmt
              | "pass" NEWLINE | assert_stmt | fn_decl | expr NEWLINE ;
exit_stmt     = exit [ "if" expr ] NEWLINE ;           (* postfix guard: one line, no else;
                                                           an `if` right after an exit is
                                                           always a guard: write
                                                           `return (if c then a else b)` *)
exit          = "return" [ expr ] | "break" [ IDENT ] | "continue" [ IDENT ] ;
                (* (semantic) an `expr` statement may not have a fallible type
                   or contain fallible results (§8.4); use `?`, handle it, or `_ =` *)
binding       = [ "mut" ] pattern [ ":" type ] "=" expr NEWLINE
              | [ "mut" ] pattern [ ":" type ] "=" or_expr "otherwise" exit NEWLINE ;
                (* (semantic) a refutable pattern is allowed only in the second form.
                   `x = e` with a plain name is a *binding* when `x` is not yet
                   visible, and an *assignment* (assign_stmt) when `x` is a visible
                   `mut` binding; on a visible immutable name it is an error.
                   A name is bound once per function: no shadowing (§3.9);
                   "visible" means locals only. A pattern always binds new
                   names; the exception is a tuple made only of visible `mut`
                   names, a parallel assignment (right side evaluated first,
                   so `(a, b) = (b, a)` swaps); mixing new and existing names
                   is an error.
                   Constructor patterns start with an uppercase name (§3.5), so
                   `Circle(r) = …` is a pattern and `f(r) = …` is not valid.
                   `let` is reserved: "`let` is not used in Verse; write `x = …`" *)
assign_stmt   = place assign_op expr NEWLINE ;
assign_op     = "=" | "+=" | "-=" | "*=" | "/=" | "%=" ;
place         = ( IDENT | "self" ) { "." IDENT | "[" expr "]" } ;

if_stmt       = "if" expr block
                { "else" "if" expr block } [ "else" block ] ;
loop_stmt     = [ IDENT ":" ] ( for_stmt | while_stmt ) ;          (* loop label *)
for_stmt      = "for" pattern "in" expr block ;
while_stmt    = "while" expr block ;
with_stmt     = "with" resource { "," resource } block ;
resource      = expr "as" [ "mut" ] IDENT ;  (* (semantic) expr's type must implement
                                           Cleanup; a fallible acquisition needs `?`;
                                           the name is mutable only with `mut` *)
assert_stmt   = "assert" expr [ "," expr ] NEWLINE ;
test_block    = "test" TEXT block ;

(* ---------- Pattern matching ---------- *)
match_expr    = "match" expr NEWLINE INDENT arm { arm } DEDENT
              | "match" NEWLINE INDENT cond_arm { cond_arm } "_" "->" arm_body DEDENT ;
                                                        (* subject-less: final `_` required *)
cond_arm      = arm_expr "->" arm_body ;                (* a Bool; `expr - lambda`, so a
                                                           lone name is not a lambda *)
arm_body      = ( arm_expr | exit | "pass" | place assign_op expr ) NEWLINE | block ;
                                                        (* `_ -> pass`, `none -> return 0`,
                                                           `x -> total += 1` *)
arm           = top_pat [ "if" arm_expr ] "->" arm_body ;
arm_expr      = expr - lambda ;          (* a lambda body must be parenthesized *)
top_pat       = ( "_" | IDENT ) ":" type                       (* typed: top level only *)
              | pattern ;
pattern       = present_pat { "|" present_pat } ;
present_pat   = single_pat { "?" } ;                           (* `user?`, `e?`, `none?` *)
single_pat    = literal | "none" | "_" | IDENT
              | TYPE_IDENT [ "(" [ sub_pats ] ")" ]            (* variant / record *)
              | "(" pattern "," pattern { "," pattern } ")"    (* tuple   *)
              | "[" [ list_pats ] "]"                          (* list    *)
              | literal ( ".." | "..=" ) literal ;             (* range   *)
sub_pats      = sub_pat { "," sub_pat } ;
sub_pat       = IDENT ":" [ field_pat ]       (* always a field; `name:` alone puns *)
              | pattern ;                     (* positional *)
field_pat     = IDENT ":" type | pattern ;    (* `body: b: Text` = typed binding *)
list_pats     = pattern { "," pattern } [ "," ".." IDENT ] | ".." IDENT ;

(* ---------- Expressions ---------- *)
expr          = lambda | cond_expr | otherwise_expr ;
lambda        = lambda_params "->" ( expr | block ) ;
                (* closing rule: a block lambda opened inside "(" on the same line
                   must be the last argument; its DEDENT also closes that "(" *)
lambda_params = IDENT | "(" [ IDENT [ ":" type ] { "," IDENT [ ":" type ] } ] ")" ;
cond_expr     = "if" expr "then" expr "else" expr ;      (* one-line conditional *)
otherwise_expr= or_expr { "otherwise" fallback } [ "otherwise" exit ] ;
                                                         (* fallback, loosest; an exit
                                                            only as the whole last operand *)
fallback      = postfix | "-" ( INT | FLOAT ) ;          (* literal, call, name, field,
                                                            index, lifted chain, ( … );
                                                            anything else: add brackets *)
or_expr       = and_expr { "or" and_expr } ;             (* Bool only *)
and_expr      = not_expr { "and" not_expr } ;
not_expr      = "not" not_expr | comparison ;
comparison    = range_expr { comp_op range_expr }
              | range_expr "is" top_pat ;
comp_op       = "==" | "!=" | "<" | "<=" | ">" | ">=" | "in" | "not" "in" ;
range_expr    = additive [ ( ".." | "..=" ) additive ] ;  (* both ends required *)
additive      = term { ( "+" | "-" ) term } ;
term          = unary { ( "*" | "/" | "%" ) unary } ;
unary         = "-" unary
              | "spawn" postfix          (* (semantic) the postfix must end in a call *)
              | power ;
power         = postfix [ "**" unary ] ; (* right-assoc; tighter than unary minus *)
postfix       = TYPE_IDENT "." IDENT type_args call { postfix_op }
              | primary { postfix_op } ;
postfix_op    = call | index | "." ( IDENT | INT | TYPE_IDENT ) | "?" ;
                (* (semantic) lifted chains: a "." on a `T?` looks through the
                   optional only when the chain is consumed by `otherwise`, a
                   postfix "?", an `is` / `match` subject, or a position whose
                   expected type is optional (§8.1); it short-circuits on the
                   first `none` and yields one flattened `?` level. Elsewhere a
                   "." on a `T?` is an error. There is no `?.` token. *)
                (* `. TYPE_IDENT`: qualified names such as `Shape.Circle(2.0)`
                   and `time.Duration` *)
                (* `TYPE_IDENT . IDENT type_args call`: explicit type arguments
                   only on an associated-function call whose receiver is a
                   capitalised type name, as in `Channel.new<Int>(capacity: 10)`;
                   a lowercase receiver never takes them, so `a.b < c > (d)` is
                   always a chained comparison. Free generic functions take no
                   explicit type arguments in 0.1 (§10.5). They are normally inferred
                   from an annotation instead:
                   `(tx, rx): (Sender<Int>, Receiver<Int>) = Channel.new(capacity: 10)` *)
                (* (semantic) postfix "?" is an ordinary postfix operator applied
                   left to right, but a "?" immediately followed by "." is an
                   error ("`?.` is not Verse"): write `(f(x)?).email` to
                   propagate then read *)
                (* (semantic) no two postfix "?" in a row: write (x?)? *)
                (* x.f(y) may call a free function f(x, y) (uniform call syntax);
                   a method always wins; ambiguity is an error *)
call          = "(" [ args ] ")" ;
args          = arg { "," arg } [ "," ] ;
arg           = IDENT ":" [ expr ]       (* named; `name:` alone puns `name: name` *)
              | [ "mut" ] expr ;         (* `mut` marks an exclusive borrow *)
index         = "[" ( expr | slice ) "]" ;
slice         = additive ( ".." | "..=" ) [ additive ]    (* open end: only in slices *)
              | ( ".." | "..=" ) additive ;

primary       = literal | IDENT | "self" | TYPE_IDENT [ type_args ]
              | "(" expr ")" | tuple | list | map | set
              | if_expr | match_expr | key_path ;
key_path      = "." ( IDENT | INT ) { "." ( IDENT | INT ) | call } ;
                (* only where an expression starts: after "(", "," or an operator;
                   plain access chains only *)
if_expr       = "if" expr block "else" ( block | if_expr ) ;   (* block form *)
tuple         = "(" arg "," [ arg { "," arg } ] [ "," ] ")" ;
list          = "[" [ elem { "," elem } [ "," ] ] "]" ;
elem          = ".." expr | expr ;                             (* prefix `..` spreads *)
map           = "{" ":" "}"                                    (* empty map; `{}` is an error *)
              | "{" entry { "," entry } [ "," ] "}" ;
entry         = ".." expr | expr ":" expr ;                    (* later keys win *)
set           = "set" "{" [ elem { "," elem } [ "," ] ] "}" ;  (* `set` is reserved *)
literal       = INT | FLOAT | TEXT | RAW_TEXT | CHAR | BYTES
              | "true" | "false" | "none" ;

Lexical tokens, informally:

(* The first character decides the kind of name (§3.5).                     *)
TYPE_IDENT  = upper { letter | digit | "_" } ;        (* upper = Unicode Lu or Lt  *)
IDENT       = ( other_letter | "_" ) { letter | digit | "_" } ;
                          (* other_letter = any letter that is not Lu/Lt,
                             including lowercase and uncased letters (e.g. 数) *)
INT         = digits | "0x" hex { hex | "_" }
            | "0o" oct { oct | "_" } | "0b" bin { bin | "_" } ;
FLOAT       = digits "." digits [ exponent ]
            | digits exponent ;                        (* 3.14, 6.02e23, 1e-9 *)
              (* right after ".", a digit sequence is always one INT, never a
                 FLOAT: `t.0.1` is INT 0 then INT 1. `10.seconds()` is INT 10,
                 ".", IDENT; `10.` with no digit after the dot is an error *)
exponent    = ( "e" | "E" ) [ "+" | "-" ] digits ;
digits      = digit { digit | "_" } ;
TEXT        = '"' { char | escape | interp } '"'
            | '"""' NEWLINE { line } '"""' ;
interp      = "{" expr [ ":" format ] "}" ;
                          (* (semantic) a TEXT inside `expr` may not itself
                             contain `interp`: nesting is one level deep *)
              (* the format ":" is the first colon not inside ( ), [ ], { }
                 or a nested text literal; an expression with its own
                 top-level colon, such as `v is n: Int`, needs ( ) *)
RAW_TEXT    = 'r"' { char } '"' | 'r"""' NEWLINE { line } '"""' ;
CHAR        = "'" ( char | escape ) "'" ;
